species.description: These nomadic acrobats can temporarily store seeds totaling up to 10% of their body weight in a special throat pouch called a crop, giving them enough energy to survive 5-6 hours of subzero temperatures. Pine Siskins are extreme cold-weather champions, ramping up their metabolism to 40% higher than normal songbirds, and can accelerate it up to five times normal when temperatures plunge to -94°F. They're unpredictable wanderers that may monopolize your feeder one winter and disappear the next, following seed crops in massive 'irruptive' movements across the continent. These tiny finches are amazing acrobats, often hanging upside down from branch tips to reach conifer cones, flashing their distinctive yellow wing markings as they flutter and feed.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These Pacific Northwest specialists build nests that are 50% fur and hair, collecting deer, rabbit, and coyote fur to create a cozy centimeter-thick blanket that covers their eggs whenever they leave the nest. They're the only chickadee species found on British Columbia's islands and are considered the most vibrant of all chickadees with their stunning chestnut backs. Like other chickadees, they use nocturnal hypothermia to survive harsh winters, conserving up to 32% of their energy by lowering their body temperature at night. These social birds often travel in mixed feeding flocks with bushtits, warblers, and nuthatches, and have readily adapted to suburban life in places like the San Francisco Bay Area.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: Originally native only to western North America, these birds rapidly spread across the continent after a 1939 pet store release on Long Island, now competing with native species in many areas. Males get their stunning red coloration from carotenoids in their diet—the same pigments found in carrots and tomatoes—and females prefer the brightest, most well-fed mates. They're among the strictest vegetarians in the bird world, with seeds, buds, and fruit making up 97% of their diet year-round, rarely switching to insects even during breeding season. On scorching hot days, these desert-adapted birds can drink more than their own body weight in water, often getting hydration from succulent cactus fruits and flowers.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These flying jewels perform death-defying courtship displays, with males climbing 130 feet into the air before plummeting in near-vertical dives that end with an explosive squeak just inches from their target. They're living furnaces with body temperatures of 107°F, but can enter torpor and drop their temperature to just 48°F to survive cold nights. Unlike most hummingbirds, female Anna's sport tiny red gorgets on their throats, and males have full rose-pink 'balaclavas' covering their heads rather than just throat bibs. These year-round western residents expanded their range dramatically in the 20th century thanks to exotic flowering trees planted in gardens, spreading from just Baja California to the entire Pacific Coast.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny dynamos are barely larger than hummingbirds but can survive bone-chilling -40°F nights, sometimes huddling together for warmth in their northern forests. Despite their diminutive size, they're parenting superstars that raise two massive broods each season, with females laying the second clutch while males single-handedly feed eight or nine fledglings from the first brood. Each of their nostrils is covered by a single, tiny feather—a unique adaptation among North American birds. These frenetically active birds spend their lives in constant motion, flicking through dense spruce and fir needles with their flashy lemon-yellow crowns, searching for insects with hyperactive energy that never seems to stop.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These feisty little contractors collect sticky conifer resin and plaster it around their nest hole entrance like natural caulk, with males applying it outside and females inside to keep out predators and competitors. They're master acrobats that defy gravity, walking headfirst down tree trunks and hanging upside down from branches while their nasal 'yank-yank' calls sound like tiny tin horns honking in the treetops. These aggressive home defenders will chase away much larger birds including woodpeckers, wrens, and even swallows, and aren't above stealing nest materials from their neighbors' homes. To avoid getting stuck in their own resin trap, they perform spectacular dives straight through the entrance hole without touching the sticky sides.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These prolific parents can raise three successful broods in a single year, though the entire population turns over every six years despite some lucky individuals living to 14 years old. They're strategic eaters with a daily schedule, consuming more earthworms in the morning and switching to fruit later in the day, and can become hilariously intoxicated when they eat too many honeysuckle berries. Winter robin roosts are absolutely massive, sometimes containing a quarter-million birds huddled together in communal sleeping arrangements. These familiar lawn-runners are actually important environmental indicators, as their ground-foraging lifestyle makes them vulnerable to pesticide poisoning, serving as early warning systems for chemical pollution in our neighborhoods.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These brilliant mimics have a massive repertoire and can perfectly imitate birds, squirrels, cats, dogs, chickens, and even mechanical objects, making them the ultimate forest impersonators. Named after Georg Steller who discovered them on an Alaskan island in 1741, they're one of only two North American jays with crests and the most frequently misspelled bird name in all of birdwatching. These intelligent corvids are habitual nest-robbers and occasional killers, sometimes attacking and killing small birds, but they're also master architects who use mud to build their nests—a technique shared only with Blue Jays. They're notorious campground bandits who size up every picnic table and backyard feeder, often caching large numbers of seeds and nuts to survive harsh mountain winters.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These brilliant problem-solvers live double lives, maintaining family territories while also joining massive communal roosts that can contain up to two million birds and have been forming in the same areas for over 100 years. They're ingenious tool-makers who fashion cups to carry water, shape wood pieces to probe for food, and even break off pine cone pieces to drop on tree climbers threatening their nests. These patient parents don't breed until they're at least two years old, with most waiting until four, and their extended families can include up to 15 individuals spanning five different generations. Despite their reputation as scavengers, they're actually crafty hunters who follow migrating songbirds to catch exhausted travelers, distract river otters to steal fish, and trail other birds to discover hidden nest locations.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These dust-bathing enthusiasts throw soil and dust over their feathers just like they're taking a water bath, sometimes creating small depressions in the ground that they'll aggressively defend against other sparrows. Introduced to Brooklyn in 1851, they've become one of the most studied birds in the world with nearly 5,000 scientific papers published about them due to their abundance and fearlessness around humans. These social birds have a strict pecking order based on the size of males' black throat patches—larger patches indicate older, more dominant birds who can avoid fights by displaying their status. They're surprisingly aggressive nest-site competitors, with historical records showing them attacking 70 different bird species, and they've been caught stealing food from robins and piercing flowers to steal nectar.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These ground-scratching specialists perform a signature 'double-scratch' move, hopping backward with both feet to uncover seeds and invertebrates in the leaf litter, and one determined individual with an injured foot was observed continuing this behavior with just one working leg. Males are singing maniacs during breeding season, spending 70-90% of their mornings belting out their buzzy songs to attract mates, but once paired up, they dramatically reduce their singing to just 5% of their time. They're living examples of continental evolution—originally one species with Eastern Towhees until ice sheets split North America, creating separate populations that eventually became distinct species. Their bold white spots may serve as natural camouflage, helping them blend into the sun-dappled undergrowth of their dry western habitats.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These 'snowbirds' are among North America's most abundant forest birds, with an estimated population of 630 million individuals spread from Alaska to Mexico and California to New York. They're the ultimate seasonal migrants, flooding south for winter across most of the eastern United States, then retreating northward each spring like a feathered tide. Their bright white outer tail feathers flash like semaphore flags as they flit through the forest understory, serving as a distinctive calling card that's visible even when the birds themselves blend into the shadows. Despite their name suggesting uniformity, Dark-eyed Juncos show remarkable variation across their range, with different subspecies displaying dramatically different color patterns from slate-gray to rusty-brown, making them a fascinating study in geographic diversity.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These memory masters can remember thousands of hiding places where they've cached seeds and food, and every autumn they literally grow new brain neurons while allowing old ones to die, essentially upgrading their mental software for winter survival. Their calls are surprisingly sophisticated language systems—the more 'dee' notes in their 'chickadee-dee-dee' call, the higher the threat level they're communicating to other birds. They're the social directors of the forest, leading mixed flocks that include nuthatches, woodpeckers, and migrating warblers, with other species relying on chickadee alarm calls even when their own species lacks similar warning systems. Despite their tiny size, they're tough enough to sleep alone in individual tree cavities even when temperatures plunge far below zero, excavating their own roosting holes in rotten wood with remarkable determination.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These silky socialites get their name from the mysterious waxy red secretions on their wing tips, whose exact function remains unknown but may help attract mates during their elaborate courtship rituals. They're living fruit detectors who can survive on fruit alone for several months, and since the 1960s some have developed orange tail tips instead of yellow from eating introduced honeysuckle berries. These dedicated architects require over 2,500 individual trips to build a single nest, though they sometimes save time by stealing materials from other birds' nests including robins and orioles. Like party-goers who've had too much to drink, Cedar Waxwings occasionally become intoxicated or even die from eating overripe, fermented berries that have started producing alcohol.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These fashion-forward finches are unusual among goldfinches in molting their body feathers twice a year, transforming from dull winter birds into brilliant yellow spring males as one of the most welcome signs of approaching warm weather. They're among the strictest vegetarians in the bird world, selecting an entirely plant-based diet and only accidentally swallowing the occasional insect, which makes them terrible foster parents for Brown-headed Cowbird chicks who can't survive on an all-seed diet. These late bloomers wait until June or July to breed—later than most North American birds—timing their nesting perfectly with when thistles and milkweeds produce the fibrous seeds they need for both nest construction and feeding their young. Paired goldfinches develop virtually identical flight calls, possibly allowing them to distinguish their mates from other couples by voice alone in large flocks.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These talented mimics weave snippets from other birds' songs into their own wheezy melodies, creating unique regional dialects that vary geographically based on which species are available to copy in each area. They're living examples of geographic variation—males in the eastern U.S. sport black backs while West Coast birds have green backs with only black caps, and south of central Mexico all males are black-backed. Despite being smaller than Lawrence's Goldfinches, these feisty birds dominate their larger cousins wherever their ranges overlap in California, eating first at feeding stations and chasing Lawrence's away from prime nesting sites. These jabbering social butterflies form mixed flocks with American Goldfinches, Pine Siskins, House Finches, and even Western Bluebirds, creating colorful clouds of yellow, green, and black that gather in scrubby oak and willow habitats.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These aerial speed demons have been recorded flying at 28 miles per hour—faster than the average traveling speed of Peregrine Falcons—while performing acrobatic stunts over lakes and streams in pursuit of flying insects. Their scientific name literally means 'fast-moving sea-green,' perfectly capturing both their incredible speed and the iridescent metallic green backs that flash purple on their rumps when caught in sunlight. These generous neighbors have been observed helping Western Bluebirds raise their young, guarding nests and tending bluebird nestlings before taking over the nest site for their own broods. Female Violet-green Swallows are strategic mothers who invest more antimicrobial proteins in later-laid eggs within a clutch, giving late-hatching chicks extra protection against infections and a better chance at survival.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny social butterflies are the only members of their family in the Americas, with seven relatives scattered across Eurasia, all sharing the remarkable ability to weave complex hanging nests shaped like soft pouches or socks. They're cooperative breeders with a twist—breeding pairs often have helpers at the nest, but unusually, these helpers are typically adult males rather than the young birds seen in most cooperative species. During breeding season, the entire Bushtit family sleeps together in their large hanging nest, but once the young fledge, they abandon the nest forever and sleep on branches like other birds. These sprightly acrobats live year-round in chattering flocks of 10 to 40 birds, constantly moving and often hanging upside down to pick insects and spiders from the undersides of leaves while twittering their way between shrubs and thickets.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These ground-loving woodpeckers break all the rules, preferring to hop around on the ground digging for ants with their unusual slightly curved bills and long barbed tongues rather than hammering on tree trunks like their relatives. They're living examples of continental evolution—the 'Red-shafted' and 'Yellow-shafted' forms were once considered separate species until scientists discovered they hybridize extensively in a wide zone from Alaska to Texas. These percussion masters drum on metal objects to make the loudest possible noise for territory defense, with one Wyoming flicker's drumming on an abandoned tractor audible from half a mile away. They're among the few strongly migratory North American woodpeckers, with northern populations moving south for winter, and they occasionally nest in the most unexpected places like old earthen burrows vacated by kingfishers or Bank Swallows.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These musical virtuosos show incredible geographic variation across North America—Aleutian Island birds are one-third longer and weigh twice as much as eastern birds, while desert Southwest birds are pale compared to the dark, heavily streaked Pacific Northwest populations. They're real estate experts with an eye for prime nesting spots, with researchers finding that certain choice locations like the base of a rose bush get used over and over again by entirely different birds across multiple years. Female Song Sparrows are attracted not just to male songs, but specifically to how well the songs reflect the male's learning ability—preferring males who better matched their song tutors and used more learned components. These prolific parents can lay up to seven clutches in a single exceptional breeding season and have successfully reared up to four clutches, making them among the most productive songbirds in North America.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These dashing sparrows are remarkable linguists—males on the edge of two song dialect regions can be bilingual, learning and singing both local dialects depending on their audience. Young males learn their songs during their first two or three months of life, not from their fathers but from the generalized song environment of their neighborhood, creating distinct regional dialects. They're incredible athletes who can run on a treadmill at one-third of a mile per hour without tiring, and migrating individuals have been tracked moving 300 miles in a single night. These selective neighbors will peacefully share territories with Fox Sparrows but aggressively chase away Chipping Sparrows and Dark-eyed Juncos, showing they have strong opinions about their roommates.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These mischievous corvids have specialized bills perfectly adapted for their oak woodland lifestyle—stout and hooked to give them extra power and grip for hammering open acorns, unlike their Woodhouse's Scrub-Jay cousins who have thinner bills for extracting pine nuts. They're helpful partners to mule deer, standing on their backs to eat ticks and parasites while the deer stand still and hold up their ears to give the jays better access. These clever thieves have been caught stealing acorns from Acorn Woodpecker caches and even stealing acorns they've watched other jays hide, but when hiding their own treasures, they're paranoid enough to check that no other jays are watching. Their calls are legendary among naturalists, with one 1923 description noting their 'dzweep, dzweep' sound 'curdles the blood, as it is meant to do.'
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These hyperactive master vocalists learn their signature songs between 30 and 60 days old from neighboring adult males rather than their fathers, developing unique melodies with notes changed here and syllables there that will be theirs for life. Named after British engraver Thomas Bewick, they were first described by John James Audubon in 1821, who noted how they moved along fence bars 'with tail generally erect, looking from bar to bar and catching spiders and insects in quick succession.' These monogamous pairs often forage together during courtship and even after the female begins incubating, possibly helping the male prevent his partner from mating with other birds. Their decline in eastern North America coincided with House Wren expansion, as House Wrens frequently remove eggs from nest cavities, demonstrating how the increased availability of nest boxes may have inadvertently helped one species while harming another.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These remarkable colonizers reached North America through an unlikely origin story—several birds escaped from a Bahamian pet shop during a mid-1970s burglary, with the shop owner then releasing the remaining 50 doves, leading to the rapid colonization of most of North America within just a few decades. Their species name 'decaocto' comes from Greek mythology about a servant girl named Decaocto who was transformed into a dove by the gods to escape unhappy treatment, with the dove's mournful cry recalling her former life. Unlike most birds, they can drink 'head down' by submerging their bills and sucking water like drinking through a straw, rather than scooping and tipping their heads back. These devoted parents feed their newly hatched chicks a fat- and protein-rich 'crop milk'—a whitish fluid from liquid-filled cells that slough off the lining of their crop—before switching to regurgitated seeds after 5-10 days.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These heavyset finches are songbirds without a song—they don't use complex sounds to attract mates or defend territory, relying instead on simple calls including sweet, piercing notes and burry chirps. Their enormous bills can crush seeds too large for smaller finches to open, creating a feeding partnership where Common Redpolls and Pine Siskins follow grosbeaks to glean the food scraps they leave behind. Though they're ferocious seed-crackers in winter, they become forest protectors in summer by eating spruce budworm caterpillars so effectively that their presence often provides the first warning of a budworm outbreak. These irregular migrants underwent a remarkable eastward expansion from the mid-1800s, when they were rare east of the Rockies, reaching Rhode Island by 1910 and becoming regular New England winter visitors by the 1920s, possibly aided by the growing number of ornamental box elder trees.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny woodland sprites are so perfectly camouflaged that naturalist W.M. Tyler described them as looking 'like a fragment of detached bark that is defying the law of gravitation by moving upward over the trunk.' They're incredibly energy-efficient, burning only 4-10 calories per day—so efficient that eating a single spider gives them enough energy to climb nearly 200 feet vertically. These architectural innovators build hammock-like nests behind loosened flaps of bark on dead trees, a unique nesting strategy that wasn't discovered by naturalists until 1879, and in Arizona they often construct nests with two openings—a downward-facing entrance and an upward-facing exit. Despite their tiny size, they're surprisingly adaptable builders, sometimes nesting in unusual places like behind window shutters, inside fence posts, or even in specially constructed boxes made of Douglas-fir bark pieces.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These flashy corvids are master architects who build enormous nests that can take up to 40 days to construct, yet remarkably use only 1% of the pair's daily energy expenditure, while laying eggs takes a whopping 23% of the female's energy budget. They're historical partners with humans—Plains Indians knew them as bold camp followers who would enter tents to steal food, and Lewis and Clark reported the same fearless behavior during their expedition. These helpful tick-removers frequently pick parasites from the backs of large mammals like deer and moose, but surprisingly they cache most of the ticks alive and unharmed rather than eating them immediately. Despite their reputation as nest predators, eggs and nestlings make up only a tiny portion of their diet, and they're actually quite social creatures who gather in numbers to feed at carrion while keeping up a constant stream of raucous calls.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These impressive waterfowl practice 'assortative mating,' with birds of both sexes choosing mates of similar size, and they're so devoted that pairs often stay together for life while raising their goslings as a family unit. The 'giant' Canada Goose subspecies was nearly driven extinct in the early 1900s but recovery programs were so successful that they've become urban nuisances in many areas, with some populations no longer migrating south due to abundant waste grain and milder winters. These remarkable navigators make annual northward molting migrations even when they're 'resident' populations, with some individuals traveling over 1,500 kilometers to take advantage of vegetation in earlier growth stages. Their size varies dramatically across their range—northern subspecies are smaller and darker western birds, with the four smallest forms now considered a separate species called the Cackling Goose.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These aerial acrobats are among the smartest birds on Earth, capable of flying upside down for over half a mile and performing rolls and somersaults while young birds play games by dropping sticks and diving to catch them mid-air. They're strategic thinkers who understand cause and effect—during hunting season, they respond to gunshots by investigating for carcasses while ignoring equally loud but harmless sounds like car doors slamming. These cunning predators sometimes work in pairs to raid seabird colonies, with one bird distracting incubating adults while the other steals eggs or chicks, and they've been observed waiting in trees as ewes give birth to attack newborn lambs. Ravens are legendary tricksters in cultures worldwide, from Edgar Allan Poe's ominous 'nevermore' to Pacific Northwest tales of ravens stealing fire from the sun, and when raised in captivity they can mimic human words and other bird calls with remarkable accuracy.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These petite olive-and-yellow flycatchers are part of a fascinating taxonomic story—in 2023, ornithologists reunited Pacific-slope and Cordilleran Flycatchers back into a single species called Western Flycatcher after treating them as separate species since 1989, showing how scientific understanding evolves. They're habitat specialists who prefer shaded forests with flowing water, particularly canyons and ravines where gaps in the canopy create perfect bug-filled hunting grounds for their flycatching lifestyle. The Channel Islands population off southern California may actually be a distinct species entirely, as these birds are larger than mainland relatives with longer bills, paler chests, different vocalizations, and distinct genetics. Like many Empidonax flycatchers, voice is the key to finding and identifying them, as males sing sharp songs and call notes frequently during the first few weeks of nesting season.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny brown songsters are considered a 'pinnacle of song complexity' by researchers, with their entire bodies shaking as they deliver tinkling, bubbly songs while holding their tails upright in the dark understory of old-growth forests. They're part of a fascinating taxonomic split—until 2010, Pacific Wrens were considered the same species as Winter Wrens, but research revealed that western birds differed from eastern and European populations, leading to the creation of three separate species. These resourceful builders have males who construct multiple nests within their territory, then lead females on tours to let them choose which nest to use for raising their young. They're surprisingly social in cold weather, with 31 individuals once found huddled together in a single nest box in western Washington, and they're opportunistic feeders who congregate near streams during salmon runs to feast on the insects attracted to salmon carcasses.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These graceful speed demons can fly at bullet-straight speeds while their wings create a distinctive sharp whistling sound during takeoff, and they're surprisingly efficient eaters who can pack a record-breaking 17,200 bluegrass seeds into their expandable crop in a single feeding session. They're desert survivors who can drink brackish spring water up to almost half the salinity of seawater without becoming dehydrated like humans would, and they consume 12-20% of their body weight daily—about 71 calories. These devoted parents feed their chicks 'crop milk,' a protein-rich fluid produced in their throat, and during breeding season you might see three doves flying in tight formation—a male leading, followed by a rival male he's chasing away, and his mate tagging along for the aerial drama. Despite being the most hunted game bird in North America with over 20 million harvested annually, they remain incredibly abundant with a U.S. population estimated at 350 million birds.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These progressive parents break traditional gender roles, with showy males sharing equally in incubating eggs and feeding young despite their flashy black, white, and cinnamon plumage that makes them conspicuous targets. They're one of the few birds that can safely eat toxic monarch butterflies during winter in central Mexico, feeding on them in roughly 8-day cycles to give their bodies time to eliminate the poisonous compounds that make monarchs deadly to most other birds. These late bloomers don't achieve their full adult breeding plumage until they're two years old, with first-year males varying from female-like to nearly adult-like, and only the most adult-looking yearlings can successfully defend territories and breed. Female Black-headed Grosbeaks are clever vocalists who occasionally sing full 'male' songs, possibly to deceive their mates about intruders and convince them to spend more time at the nest helping with parental duties.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These prolific hybridizers are the ancestors of nearly all domestic duck breeds and are notorious for interbreeding with at least eight other duck species, creating identification challenges for birders worldwide. They're speed demons of the sky, with migrating flocks clocked at 55 miles per hour, and they undergo a dramatic transformation during molting season when they shed all flight feathers and become flightless for 3-4 weeks while growing secretive 'eclipse' plumage. These early planners form pairs in fall for the following spring's breeding season, but males are notorious for pursuing 'extra-pair copulations,' often forcing themselves on females in aggressive group chases. The classic duck 'quack' that everyone knows is actually only made by female Mallards—males produce a quieter, rasping sound instead of the iconic quack we associate with all ducks.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These flame-colored beauties are living chemistry experiments—their brilliant red head feathers get their color from rhodoxanthin, a rare pigment they can't produce themselves but must obtain from insects in their diet, making them one of the few birds whose red coloration doesn't come from common plant carotenoids. They're the northernmost tanagers in the world, breeding as far north as Canada's Northwest Territories at 60 degrees latitude, where they may spend only two months before beginning their southward migration. These acrobatic courtship performers put on spectacular displays where males tumble past females with their yellow and black plumage flashing dramatically through the air. Around 1900, they were considered serious agricultural pests, with one observer reporting that cherry orchard damage was so severe that 'the sales of the fruit which was left did not balance the bills paid out for poison and ammunition,' though today they're protected and recognized as beneficial insect-eaters.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These remarkable vocal mimics can learn the calls of up to 20 different bird species, copying everything from Eastern Wood-Pewees to Red-tailed Hawks with stunning accuracy, and they're speed demons capable of flying at 48 mph. They're living fashion shows that change their appearance twice yearly without molting—their spotted winter plumage transforms to glossy dark breeding colors as the white feather tips simply wear away in a process scientists call 'wear molt.' These successful colonizers exploded from just a few Central Park introductions in the 1890s to an estimated 93 million birds ranging from Alaska to Mexico, making them one of North America's most numerous songbirds. They're sophisticated taste-testers who can distinguish between different types of sugars and detect salt, citric acid, and bitter tannins, though they lack the ability to digest table sugar despite being able to taste it.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These 'sparrows dipped in raspberry juice,' as Roger Tory Peterson famously described them, are sophisticated seed processors who use their big beaks and tongues to crush seeds and extract the nutritious nut inside, and they perform similar tricks to get nectar without eating entire flowers. They're talented vocal mimics who weave the sounds of other species into their rich warbling songs, including Barn Swallows, American Goldfinches, Eastern Towhees, and Brown-headed Cowbirds. These irregular wanderers move erratically from year to year, and they're losing ground in eastern North America to House Finches, losing out in over 95% of encounters between the two species since House Finches were introduced to New York City in the 1950s. From a plant's perspective, these chunky finches are actually predators rather than helpful seed dispersers—while fruit-eating birds help plants by spreading seeds, Purple Finches eat the seeds themselves, marking the end of the line for those potential new plants.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These cobalt-blue aerial acrobats are the most abundant and widely distributed swallow species in the world, breeding throughout the Northern Hemisphere and wintering in much of the Southern Hemisphere with their distinctive deeply forked tails streaming behind them. They're architectural innovators who once nested exclusively in caves throughout North America but now build their cup-shaped mud nests almost exclusively on human-made structures, with only the Channel Islands population off California still regularly using natural cave sites. These sometimes ruthless competitors include unmated males who may kill the nestlings of nesting pairs to break up the bond and gain mating opportunities with the female. According to ancient legend, Barn Swallows got their forked tails when they stole fire from the gods to bring to humans—an angry deity hurled a firebrand at the swallow, singeing away its middle tail feathers forever.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These iridescent blue-green aerialists are among the best-studied bird species in North America, helping researchers make major advances in ecology, yet we still know surprisingly little about their lives during migration and winter. They're remarkable survivors who winter farther north than any other American swallows and return to nesting grounds long before other swallows, surviving cold snaps by eating plant foods like bayberry when insects aren't available. These social roosters create spectacular natural tornadoes when migrating flocks numbering in the hundreds of thousands gather an hour before sunset, swirling in dense clouds above cattail marshes before dropping down to roost. Despite being called Tree Swallows, they're most often seen in open, treeless areas—their name comes from their habit of nesting in tree cavities, though they readily accept nest boxes and have become backyard favorites for their acrobatic insect-catching displays.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny acrobats are North America's smallest woodpecker, barely larger than a nuthatch, yet they're surprisingly resourceful foragers who can balance on slender plant galls and sycamore seed balls to extract insects that larger woodpeckers can't reach. They're social strategists who join mixed-species winter flocks with chickadees and nuthatches, spending less time watching for predators and more time finding food thanks to their feathered companions. These gender-role specialists divide up foraging territories by sex—males work the smaller branches and weed stems while females are relegated to larger branches and trunks, but when researchers remove males from an area, females quickly move into the more productive small-branch territories. Unlike their drumming for communication, which creates loud rhythmic sounds on wood or metal, Downy Woodpeckers make surprisingly little noise while actually feeding, even when digging vigorously into wood for insects.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These ventriloquial singers produce haunting, upward-spiraling flute songs that can seem to come from multiple directions at once, as the birds move quickly between perches or their songs reverberate through dense forest foliage. They're nicknamed 'mosquito thrushes' for their flycatching habit of sallying out from perches to catch flying insects, though they also bound across the forest floor to hunt prey and pluck berries from branches. These long-distance migrants have two distinct populations—the 'russet-backed' Pacific birds that winter in Central America and the 'olive-backed' interior birds that travel all the way to South America. They're ingenious nest builders who often line their nests with horsehair fungus filaments that have natural antibiotic properties, helping protect their young from harmful pathogens.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds
Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute

species.description: These tiny fierce predators are practically bursting with attitude despite being only robin-sized—they're silent death to mice and small mammals, usually eating adult mice in pieces over the course of two meals. They're mysterious migrants whose movements were poorly understood until the 1990s when Project Owlnet began using their distinctive 'too-too-too' calls to lure them into mist nets, revealing that they can cross the Great Lakes and even land on fishing vessels 70 miles from shore in the Atlantic Ocean. These dedicated parents have unusual family dynamics—females do all incubation and brooding while males hunt, but when the youngest nestling reaches 18 days old, the female abandons the nest entirely, leaving the male to continue feeding while older siblings help care for younger ones. They're surprisingly messy housekeepers whose nest cavities accumulate thick layers of feces, pellets, and rotting prey parts by the time the young fledge, creating quite a contrast to the female's earlier meticulous cleaning.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny mountain acrobats are incredibly efficient eaters who need only 10 calories per day to survive—equivalent to about one-twentieth of an ounce of peanut butter—yet they can pack away 275 tiny caterpillars in their stomach during insect outbreaks. They're strategic food hoarders who shell sunflower seeds by holding them between their feet and hammering them apart with their beaks before flying off to stash them for later. These high-altitude specialists have evolved longer incubation periods than their Black-capped Chickadee cousins, taking almost a full week longer to hatch their eggs, possibly because they nest in harder-walled trees that provide better protection from predators. They're the social nucleus of mixed mountain bird flocks, flitting through high branches and hanging upside down to pluck insects and seeds from cones while giving their scolding 'chick-a-dee' calls to anyone who will listen.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These apex predators have talons so powerful that when clenched, they require 28 pounds of force to open, and they use this deadly grip to sever the spines of large prey including raptors like Ospreys and Peregrine Falcons. They're one of the few predators that regularly hunts skunks, and they can take down birds and mammals even larger than themselves while also dining on tiny scorpions, mice, and frogs. These silent hunters are covered in extremely soft feathers that insulate them against cold weather and allow them to fly virtually soundlessly, with short, wide wings perfect for maneuvering through forest trees. Despite the female being larger than her mate, the male has a bigger voice box and deeper voice, and pairs often call together with audible differences in pitch that create their haunting duets.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These miniature Canada Geese were only recognized as a separate species in 2004 when the four smallest subspecies were split off, creating a fascinating example of how scientific understanding evolves with new research. They're remarkably variable in size, with the smallest subspecies weighing only one-quarter as much as the largest Canada Goose subspecies—a dramatic difference of up to 11 pounds between the extremes. These high-pitched callers get their name from their distinctively cackling voice, which is noticeably different from the deeper honking of Canada Geese and helps birders distinguish them in mixed flocks. They're diverse nesters who adapt to different environments—most nest along tundra ponds and streams, but the Aleutian subspecies nests on south-facing turf slopes above sea cliffs, while Richardson's subspecies can form colonies of several hundred pairs on steep rock slopes.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These grayish-brown flycatchers are living mysteries whose exact winter destinations in northern South America remain unknown because they look so similar to Eastern Wood-Pewees and rarely call on their wintering grounds. They're remarkable examples of reproductive isolation—despite their breeding ranges overlapping in a narrow Great Plains zone and being nearly identical to Eastern Wood-Pewees, no evidence has ever been found of interbreeding, likely because their songs sound so different. These precision hunters put on aerial shows from exposed branches, sallying back and forth to nab flying insects with stunning accuracy while making clapping noises with their bills when defending their nests from intruders. Their scientific name tells their story perfectly: 'Contopus' means 'short foot' in Greek, referring to their relatively short legs, while 'sordidulus' means 'dirty or unkempt,' describing the dusky brown wash across their breast and flanks.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These master actors are famous for their 'broken-wing' display, dramatically dragging a wing and crying pitifully to lure predators away from their nests, but they use completely different tactics against large hoofed animals—fluffing up, displaying their tail over their head, and charging at cows or horses to make them change course. They're surprisingly aquatic for a 'dry land' shorebird, with adults swimming well in swift-flowing water and chicks able to swim across small streams when necessary. These obsessive decorators engage in elaborate nest-building rituals where mated pairs perform 'scrape ceremonies,' and they continuously add materials to their nests by picking up items and tossing them over their shoulders—one Oklahoma nest accumulated over 1,500 pebbles this way. Despite being common on lawns and parking lots, they can be surprisingly dangerous urban nesters, with some chicks surviving leaps from seven-story buildings when they're unable to leave gravel rooftops due to high parapets and screened drains.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These aerial daredevils perform one of nature's most dramatic courtship displays, diving from above the treetops at breakneck speed before pulling out just meters from the ground, creating a deep booming sound as air rushes across their flexed wingtips like a racecar passing by. They're ancient wanderers with Late Pleistocene fossils up to 400,000 years old found across North America, and they have one of the longest migration routes of all North American birds, sometimes showing up as far off course as Iceland, Greenland, and the British Isles. These misnamed 'bullbats' are neither strictly nocturnal nor related to hawks—they're active at dawn and dusk, earning their colloquial name from their erratic, bat-like flight combined with their impressive booming courtship sounds. They're master camouflagers who make no nest at all, laying their eggs directly on bare ground where both adults and young seem to vanish the moment they land, blending perfectly with their surroundings.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny sparrows were once known as 'hair birds' because they line their nests with animal hair, particularly horsehair when it was readily available in rural America, creating some of the softest nest linings in the bird world. They're mechanical musicians whose rapid, dry trill songs sound like an old-fashioned sewing machine or a car engine that won't quite start, and males can repeat this monotonous trill for minutes at a time from prominent perches. These early migrants are among the first sparrows to return in spring, when their distinctive rusty caps and clear white eyebrow stripes make them easy to identify as they forage on the ground beneath feeders. They're surprisingly social during winter, forming large flocks that can number in the hundreds as they roam through open woodlands and brushy areas searching for seeds.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These notorious brood parasites are North America's most common 'deadbeat parents,' with females laying their eggs in the nests of over 220 different host species and never building a nest or raising their own young. They evolved this lifestyle following massive buffalo herds across the Great Plains, feeding on insects stirred up by the hooves, which made it impossible to stay in one place long enough to raise a family. These strategic egg-layers can produce up to 40 eggs per season, often removing or destroying host eggs before laying their own, and their chicks typically hatch earlier and grow faster than their foster siblings. Originally called 'buffalo birds,' they've dramatically expanded their range as forests were cleared and cattle replaced bison, creating new opportunities for their parasitic lifestyle while unfortunately impacting many songbird species that lack defenses against nest parasitism.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny warriors are considered the most aggressive of all hummingbirds, fearlessly attacking birds many times their size and even chasing away hawks, eagles, and other large birds from their territories with relentless determination. They're incredible long-distance migrants who travel up to 4,000 miles between their breeding grounds in Alaska and wintering areas in Mexico, making one of the longest migrations relative to body size of any bird in the world. These memory masters have excellent spatial recall and can remember the exact locations of hundreds of flowers and feeders across their territory, returning to check each one on a regular schedule even if it's been empty for days. Despite weighing only about as much as a penny, males perform spectacular courtship dives, plummeting from heights of 100 feet or more while their tail feathers create a distinctive buzzing sound that can be heard from considerable distances.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These handsome sparrows are famous for their melancholy three-note song that sounds like 'oh-dear-me' or 'I'm-so-tired,' earning them folk names like the 'weary bird' from early settlers who found the descending whistle particularly poignant. They're social winter visitors who form large mixed flocks along the Pacific coast, often joining White-crowned Sparrows and other species as they forage through weedy lots, city edges, and shrubby lowlands. These long-distance migrants breed in remote areas of Alaska and western Canada, making them one of the least-studied North American sparrows during breeding season due to the inaccessibility of their nesting grounds. They're surprisingly hardy birds who can withstand harsh coastal winter weather, and their distinctive golden crown stripes bordered by black make them one of the most striking sparrows when seen in good light.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These medium-sized woodpeckers are the classic 'big brother' to Downy Woodpeckers, looking nearly identical but with bills as long as their heads and completely white outer tail feathers, while Downies have shorter bills and black-spotted white tail feathers. They're surprisingly variable across their range, with western populations being darker and Pacific Northwest birds having less white on their backs, leading to nine recognized subspecies from Alaska to Central America. These powerful excavators prefer larger trees than their smaller cousins and can hammer through thick bark to reach wood-boring beetle larvae, making them important forest health indicators since they concentrate where insect damage is most severe. They're devoted parents who take turns incubating eggs in shifts, with males typically taking the night shift, and both parents feed their young by regurgitating insects directly into their mouths for the first few days after hatching.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These golden-breasted songsters are famous for their flute-like songs that can carry for over a mile across open grasslands, with each male knowing 8-12 different song types and switching between them to avoid boring their neighbors. They're ground-dwelling architects who build dome-shaped nests with side entrances, often weaving a tunnel through the grass that leads to the nest entrance like a secret passageway. These opportunistic nesters have been found raising their young in some unusual places, including the middle of golf course fairways where they somehow manage to avoid mowers and golfers. Despite being called 'larks,' they're actually members of the blackbird family, and their scientific name 'neglecta' comes from the fact that early ornithologists overlooked them for decades, assuming they were the same species as Eastern Meadowlarks until 1844.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These adaptable coastal scavengers are the most common large gull along the Pacific Northwest coast and have learned to thrive in urban environments, regularly seen at garbage dumps, parking lots, and fast-food restaurants where they've mastered the art of stealing french fries. They're opportunistic predators who hunt everything from fish and crabs to small mammals and birds, and they've been observed using tools like bread to bait fish and dropping shellfish from great heights onto rocks to crack them open. These social nesters form large colonies on offshore islands and coastal cliffs, where they can live over 20 years and return to the same nesting sites year after year with remarkable site fidelity. They're prolific hybridizers who readily interbreed with other gull species, particularly Western Gulls, creating identification challenges for birders as the hybrid offspring can show a bewildering array of intermediate characteristics.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These stunning orange-and-black thrushes are the 'spirits of the old-growth forest,' producing haunting single-note songs that echo through misty Pacific Northwest woodlands like ethereal flute calls from another world. They're surprisingly nomadic birds whose winter movements are unpredictable—some years they appear in large numbers far outside their normal range, showing up in backyards across the continent from Texas to Nova Scotia, while other years they seem to vanish entirely. These ground-foraging specialists use a distinctive 'double-scratch' technique, jumping forward and then quickly scratching backward with both feet to uncover insects, worms, and seeds hidden in the forest duff. They're devoted parents who build their cup-shaped nests on horizontal branches of conifers, often 15-20 feet high, and the female does all the incubating while the male stands guard and brings her food during the 12-day incubation period.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These hardy warblers are the only members of their family that can digest the waxy coating on bayberries and wax myrtle fruits, allowing them to winter much farther north than other warblers who must migrate to find insects. They're living examples of recent evolution in action—the 'Myrtle' and 'Audubon's' forms were considered separate species until 1973, when scientists discovered they hybridize extensively in a narrow zone through the Canadian Rockies. These acrobatic insect-catchers are surprisingly versatile, hawking flies like flycatchers, gleaning insects from bark like nuthatches, and even hovering briefly to pick insects from foliage tips. They're among the most abundant warblers in North America, with an estimated population of 130 million birds, and their distinctive 'butter-butt' yellow rump patch flashes like a beacon as they flit through trees during migration.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These polygamous males are among North America's most studied birds, with some individuals maintaining territories containing up to 15 different females, though most average 2-3 mates per breeding season. They're fierce defenders who will attack much larger birds including hawks, crows, and even humans who venture too close to their nests, with males spreading their wings to flash their bright red shoulder patches while giving harsh alarm calls. These adaptable colonizers have expanded their range dramatically as humans created more wetland edges and agricultural areas, and they're now among the most abundant birds in North America with an estimated population of 190 million. They're surprisingly long-lived for songbirds, with the oldest known wild individual reaching at least 15 years and 9 months, and they form massive winter roosts that can contain millions of birds creating spectacular aerial displays at dawn and dusk.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These charming ground birds are famous for their distinctive forward-curving head plumes that bob as they walk, and they're highly social creatures who live in groups called 'coveys' that can contain 25-40 individuals during fall and winter. They're devoted parents who practice 'egg dumping'—females sometimes lay eggs in other females' nests, leading to super-clutches of up to 28 eggs, though the typical clutch is 12-16 eggs. These water-wise desert dwellers can survive entirely on the moisture they get from their food, rarely needing to drink water directly, and they have specialized salt glands that help them process salty foods. They're surprisingly fast runners who prefer to escape danger on foot rather than flying, reaching speeds up to 12 mph while weaving through brush, and when they do fly, they burst into the air with explosive wingbeats before gliding on set wings.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These iridescent blackbirds are opportunistic urbanites who have learned to thrive in parking lots, shopping centers, and fast-food restaurants, where they've been observed following shoppers and waiting for dropped food with remarkable patience. They're surprisingly intelligent problem-solvers who have been seen using cars as nutcrackers, placing nuts behind vehicle tires and waiting for the cars to drive over them. These social nesters often form loose colonies where multiple pairs build their nests in the same area, and they're cooperative defenders who will mob predators together while giving harsh alarm calls. Named after ornithologist Thomas Brewer in 1844, males display their glossy purple-blue head and green body iridescence most dramatically during breeding season, while females are a more subdued brownish-gray that helps them blend in while incubating their pale blue eggs.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny yellow dynamos are among the most active warblers, constantly flicking their tails and wings while hopping through dense vegetation like hyperactive wind-up toys searching for insects. They're remarkable long-distance migrants who breed as far north as Alaska and winter in Central America, with some individuals traveling over 5,000 miles twice a year despite weighing only about as much as two pennies. These devoted parents are frequent victims of Brown-headed Cowbird parasitism, but they've evolved an unusual defense—they sometimes build a new nest floor right over the cowbird egg, effectively burying it and starting fresh. Named after pioneering ornithologist Alexander Wilson, males sport distinctive black caps that make them look like they're wearing tiny berets, while females have the same bright yellow coloration but lack the dramatic black headwear.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These crow-sized powerhouses are North America's largest woodpecker and create distinctive rectangular excavations in trees while hunting for carpenter ants, leaving behind holes so large they can weaken or even kill trees. They're living jackhammers whose heads endure forces of 1,200-1,500 Gs with each strike—impacts that would cause severe brain injury in humans—thanks to specialized skull adaptations including a reinforced bill, shock-absorbing tissues, and a brain that fits tightly in its skull. These forest architects excavate new nest cavities each year in dead trees, creating homes that are later used by Wood Ducks, owls, bats, and dozens of other species, making them crucial ecosystem engineers. Their distinctive undulating flight pattern and loud, ringing calls can be heard from over half a mile away, and their flaming red crests inspired the cartoon character Woody Woodpecker.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These subtly beautiful warblers are masters of disguise whose orange crown patch is usually completely hidden and only visible when they're excited or alarmed, making them one of the most challenging warblers to identify. They're remarkably hardy migrants who winter farther north than most other warblers, surviving cold weather by switching from insects to nectar, tree sap, and even suet at bird feeders. These versatile foragers have developed an unusual feeding behavior—they're one of the few warblers that regularly probe flowers for nectar, and they've been observed piercing the base of tubular flowers to 'steal' nectar without pollinating the plant. They're surprisingly variable across their range, with four distinct subspecies that differ dramatically in brightness and size, from the dull gray birds of the interior mountains to the bright yellow Pacific coast populations.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These fishing experts are unusual among North American birds because females are more colorful than males—females sport both blue and rusty-red belts across their chest while males have only the blue belt. They're incredible excavators who dig tunnel burrows 3-6 feet deep into riverbanks using their bills and feet, creating underground nesting chambers that can take 3-12 days of hard work to complete. These patient hunters perch motionless over water before diving headfirst at speeds up to 25 mph, and they can adjust their vision to account for light refraction in water, making them deadly accurate fishers. They're surprisingly territorial and will chase away much larger birds like herons and eagles from their fishing spots, and their loud, rattling calls can be heard from over half a mile away as they patrol their waterfront territories.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These small flycatchers are virtually impossible to distinguish from Alder Flycatchers by sight alone, but they give themselves away with their distinctive 'fitz-bew' song that sounds like a sneeze, while Alder Flycatchers say 'fee-bee-o.' They're habitat specialists who prefer dense thickets of willows, alders, and other shrubs near water, and they're considered an indicator species for healthy riparian ecosystems. These late migrants don't arrive on their breeding grounds until late May or early June, making them one of the last warblers and flycatchers to return from their Central and South American wintering areas. They're meticulous nest builders who weave together grasses, plant fibers, and spider webs to create compact cup nests, often placing them in the fork of a shrub just 2-7 feet off the ground where they're well-hidden among the dense foliage.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These adaptable raptors are North America's most common and widespread hawk, with 14 recognized subspecies that vary dramatically in coloration from nearly white to almost black, though all adults share the distinctive rusty-red tail. They're patient hunters who can sit motionless on a perch for hours waiting for the perfect moment to strike, and they have eyesight 8 times sharper than humans, allowing them to spot a mouse from over a mile away. These urban adapters have learned to thrive in cities, nesting on skyscrapers, bridges, and cell towers, and they're the hawks most commonly seen soaring over highways where they hunt rodents in the grassy medians. They're surprisingly vocal birds whose piercing 'keeeeee-arrr' scream is the classic hawk call used in movies and TV shows, even when the bird on screen is actually a different species like a Bald Eagle.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These streaky grassland sparrows are named after Savannah, Georgia, where Alexander Wilson first collected the species in 1811, but they're actually found across most of North America in open habitats from salt marshes to prairie grasslands. They're ground-dwelling specialists who run through grass like tiny mice, often staying hidden until nearly stepped on before flushing with a short, weak flight that quickly drops them back into cover. These variable birds show remarkable geographic diversity with 17 recognized subspecies, including the endangered 'Belding's' Savannah Sparrow that lives only in California salt marshes and the 'Ipswich' Savannah Sparrow that breeds exclusively on Sable Island, Nova Scotia. They're surprisingly hardy migrants, with some populations traveling from Alaska to Central America, and they navigate using the stars, magnetic fields, and polarized light patterns invisible to human eyes.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These fish-eating specialists are so uniquely adapted for their lifestyle that they're placed in their own taxonomic family, with reversible outer toes that help them grasp slippery fish, nostrils that can close underwater, and specialized scales on their feet for extra grip. They're incredible fishers with a 70% success rate when diving, plunging feet-first from heights up to 130 feet and sometimes completely submerging before emerging with fish grasped headfirst for better aerodynamics. These global wanderers are found on every continent except Antarctica, making them one of the most widely distributed birds in the world, and some individuals migrate over 160,000 miles during their lifetime. They're devoted partners who often mate for life and return to the same massive stick nests year after year, with some nests growing to over 10 feet deep and 6 feet across after decades of additions.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These small, olive-gray birds are masters of disguise who are easily confused with Ruby-crowned Kinglets, but they move more deliberately and lack the kinglet's nervous wing-flicking behavior. They're year-round residents of oak woodlands along the Pacific coast, making them one of the few vireos that don't migrate, and they're so closely tied to oak trees that their distribution almost perfectly matches that of live oaks and other oak species. These patient foragers move slowly through the canopy, carefully inspecting leaves and bark for insects, and they're known for their persistent, monotonous songs that can continue for hours with barely a pause. Named after William Hutton, a 19th-century naturalist and collector, they're surprisingly variable across their range, with some populations being much grayer while others are more olive or even yellowish, leading to ongoing debates about whether some forms might actually be separate species.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny ducks are North America's smallest dabbling duck and among the fastest flying waterfowl, reaching speeds up to 50 mph with rapid wingbeats that create a distinctive whistling sound in flight. They're incredibly agile fliers who can take off almost vertically from the water surface and perform tight aerial maneuvers that would make fighter pilots envious, often flying in compact flocks that wheel and turn in perfect synchronization. These hardy birds are among the last ducks to migrate south in fall and the first to return in spring, with some individuals able to survive in partially frozen waters by finding small areas of open water near springs or fast-moving streams. They're surface feeders who tip forward to reach submerged vegetation and seeds, and males perform elaborate courtship displays including head-bobbing, tail-wagging, and a distinctive whistle that sounds like a high-pitched 'krick-krick.'
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny acrobats are among the most social nuthatches, living in flocks of 5-15 birds year-round and even roosting together in tree cavities during cold winter nights, with up to 100 individuals sometimes packed into a single cavity for warmth. They're cooperative breeders where 'helper' birds assist the breeding pair in feeding nestlings, and these helpers are usually offspring from previous years who delay their own breeding to help their parents raise more siblings. These pine specialists are so closely tied to ponderosa pine forests that their range almost perfectly matches that of these trees, and they use their tiny bills to extract seeds from pine cones and probe bark crevices for insects. They're surprisingly vocal birds with a complex vocabulary of calls including contact notes, alarm calls, and even what appears to be 'baby talk' when communicating with nestlings, and they can often be heard chattering constantly as flocks move through the forest canopy.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These hyperactive tiny birds are constantly in motion, flicking their wings nervously every few seconds in a distinctive behavior that helps distinguish them from similar species like vireos. They're surprisingly loud singers whose complex songs can last up to 10 seconds and contain over 20 different notes, an impressive vocal performance from a bird that weighs less than a quarter of an ounce. These hardy migrants can survive temperatures as low as -40°F by entering a state of controlled hypothermia at night, lowering their body temperature by up to 20 degrees to conserve energy. The male's brilliant ruby crown patch is usually hidden and only flashed when he's excited, agitated, or trying to impress a female, and despite their tiny size, they're fearless defenders who will attack much larger birds that threaten their territory.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These magnificent raptors are one of conservation's greatest success stories, recovering from just 417 breeding pairs in 1963 to over 70,000 pairs today after DDT was banned and intensive protection efforts were implemented. They're surprisingly patient fishers who can dive at speeds up to 100 mph to snatch fish from water surfaces, but they're also notorious pirates who steal fish from Ospreys and other birds rather than catching their own. These long-lived birds don't develop their iconic white head and tail feathers until they're 4-5 years old, spending their juvenile years in mottled brown plumage that can make identification challenging. They're devoted partners who perform spectacular aerial courtship displays, cartwheeling through the sky with talons locked together, and they build some of the largest nests in North America—the record holder was 9.5 feet wide, 20 feet deep, and weighed over 2 tons.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These stocky flycatchers are long-distance migration champions who travel up to 7,000 miles from their breeding grounds in North American boreal forests to wintering areas in South America, making one of the longest migrations of any flycatcher. They're 'sit-and-wait' predators who perch conspicuously on the very tops of tall dead trees or snags, scanning for large flying insects like bees, wasps, and flying ants, which they catch in spectacular aerial sallies. These declining birds are considered an indicator species for healthy old-growth forests, as they require large territories with a mix of dense forest for nesting and open areas or clearings for hunting. Their distinctive song sounds like 'quick-three-beers' or 'hip-three-cheers,' and they're known for their aggressive territorial behavior, chasing away much larger birds including hawks and ravens that venture too close to their nesting areas.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These elegant gray thrushes are remarkable singers whose complex, flute-like songs can contain over 100 different phrases and continue for several minutes without repetition, making them among the most accomplished vocalists in North America. They're unusual among thrushes for being primarily fruit-eaters during winter, defending territories around juniper trees and other berry-producing plants with fierce determination, sometimes fighting to the death over prime feeding spots. These high-altitude specialists breed in remote mountain areas above 6,000 feet, often nesting on cliff faces or in rocky crevices where their gray plumage provides perfect camouflage against granite and limestone. Named after ornithologist John Kirk Townsend, they're surprisingly nomadic birds whose winter movements are unpredictable—some years they appear in large numbers at lower elevations, while other years they seem to vanish entirely from their usual haunts.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These bird-hunting specialists are perfectly designed for high-speed chases through dense forests, with short rounded wings and long tails that allow them to navigate tight spaces while pursuing songbirds at breakneck speeds. They're urban adapters who have learned to thrive in cities and suburbs, where they hunt at backyard bird feeders and have become so common that they're now more abundant in some urban areas than in their natural forest habitats. These patient predators often use a 'sit-and-wait' strategy, perching motionlessly for hours before launching surprise attacks, and they're known for their persistence—they'll chase prey through thick vegetation and even on foot when necessary. Named after naturalist William Cooper, females are significantly larger than males (a trait called reverse sexual dimorphism), allowing pairs to hunt different-sized prey and reduce competition between mates.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These stunning waterfowl are one of the few duck species that regularly perch and nest in trees, with females laying their eggs in tree cavities up to 65 feet high, and day-old ducklings must make a terrifying leap to the ground when they're ready to leave the nest. They're conservation success stories who nearly went extinct in the early 1900s due to overhunting and habitat loss, but thanks to nest box programs and hunting restrictions, their populations have recovered dramatically. These unique ducks have sharp claws on their webbed feet that allow them to grip bark and perch on branches, and they're among the most colorful waterfowl in North America, with males sporting iridescent green heads, white stripes, and chestnut breasts. They're surprisingly agile fliers who can navigate through dense forest canopies with ease, and they're one of the few ducks that can take off vertically from water without a running start.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These elegant flycatchers are almost always found near water, perching on low branches, rocks, or human-made structures while scanning for flying insects over streams, ponds, and irrigation ditches. They're master builders who construct their cup-shaped nests from mud pellets mixed with plant fibers, often attaching them to vertical surfaces under bridges, eaves, or cliff overhangs where they're protected from rain. These year-round residents are among the most sedentary flycatchers, with many individuals staying in the same territory throughout their lives, and they're known for their distinctive tail-pumping behavior and soft 'tsip' calls. They're surprisingly tolerant of human activity and often nest on buildings, porches, and other structures, making them one of the most urban-adapted flycatchers in North America, and their striking black and white plumage makes them unmistakable among their more drab flycatcher relatives.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These grassland sparrows get their name from their habit of singing most actively in the evening hours around vespers (evening prayers), when their sweet, melancholy songs ring across open fields and prairies. They're ground-nesters who build their cup-shaped nests in small depressions scraped into the earth, often at the base of grass clumps or small shrubs, and they're so well-camouflaged that they're nearly impossible to spot until they flush. These declining birds are indicators of healthy grassland ecosystems and have suffered dramatic population losses as prairies have been converted to agriculture and development, making them a species of conservation concern across much of their range. They're distinguished from other sparrows by their white outer tail feathers that flash conspicuously when they fly, and they have a distinctive habit of running along the ground rather than hopping like most other sparrows.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These aerial masters spend virtually their entire lives in flight, eating, drinking, mating, and even sleeping on the wing, only landing to roost and nest in hollow trees or chimneys. They're famous for creating one of nature's most spectacular roosting displays when thousands of individuals spiral down into large chimneys at dusk, creating a living tornado that can be seen from miles away. These tiny speedsters can reach speeds of 60 mph and are capable of flying backwards and hovering, making them among the most agile birds in North America, and their wings beat so rapidly they create a distinctive chittering sound. Named after William Vaux, a 19th-century mineralogist, they're closely related to Chimney Swifts but are smaller and found primarily in the Pacific Northwest, where they've adapted to using both natural tree cavities and human-made structures for nesting and roosting.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These brilliant blue cavity-nesters are cooperative breeders where young males from previous broods often help their parents raise new nestlings, bringing food and defending the territory while learning parenting skills for their own future families. They're conservation success stories who have benefited enormously from nest box programs after their populations declined due to competition with introduced House Sparrows and European Starlings for nesting cavities. These insect-hunters have excellent eyesight and can spot small prey from over 60 feet away, and they use a 'sit-and-wait' hunting strategy, perching on fence posts or low branches before dropping down to catch insects on the ground. Males are particularly striking with their deep blue heads, wings, and tails contrasting with rusty-orange breasts, while females are more subdued gray-brown with blue wings and tails, and both sexes have the characteristic upright posture typical of thrushes.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These industrious birds are nature's ultimate hoarders, creating elaborate 'granary trees' by drilling thousands of precisely-sized holes in dead trees and telephone poles, then storing individual acorns in each hole like a living pantry that can contain up to 50,000 acorns. They live in complex social groups of up to 15 individuals that cooperatively defend their granary trees and raise young together, with multiple females laying eggs in the same nest cavity and all group members helping to incubate and feed the chicks. These clown-faced woodpeckers are incredibly intelligent and have been observed moving acorns between holes as they dry and shrink, ensuring a tight fit that prevents theft by squirrels and other competitors. They're so dependent on oak trees that their range almost perfectly matches the distribution of oak forests, and they supplement their acorn diet with insects, tree sap, and occasionally eggs and nestlings of other birds.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These distinctive geese are easily recognized by their white patches around the bill and irregular black bars across their bellies that are unique to each individual, like fingerprints that allow researchers to identify specific birds from photographs.
