They're remarkable navigators who breed in the remote Arctic tundra and migrate thousands of miles to wintering grounds, with some populations traveling from Alaska to Mexico using ancient flyways passed down through generations. These social birds form large flocks during migration and winter, often mixing with other goose species, and they're known for their loud, high-pitched calls that sound like laughter, earning them the nickname 'laughing geese.' They're surprisingly long-lived for waterfowl, with some individuals reaching over 20 years old, and they show strong family bonds, with young birds often migrating with their parents for their first year of life.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These acrobatic tree-climbers are the only birds that regularly walk headfirst down tree trunks, using their powerful feet and sharp claws to defy gravity while searching for insects hidden in bark crevices that other birds miss. They're tool users who wedge large nuts and seeds into bark crevices, then hammer them open with their bills, and they're strategic food cachers who hide thousands of seeds throughout their territory and can remember the locations for months. These year-round residents are surprisingly territorial and will chase away much larger birds from their favorite trees, and they're known for their nasal 'yank-yank-yank' calls that sound like tiny horns honking. They're devoted pairs who often mate for life and maintain territories together year-round, and they have an unusual habit of 'anting'—rubbing ants on their feathers, possibly to use the formic acid as an insecticide or fungicide.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These high-altitude specialists are perfectly adapted for mountain life, with larger hearts and more efficient oxygen-carrying capacity than lowland hummingbirds, allowing them to thrive at elevations up to 10,500 feet where the air is thin. They're living metronomes whose wings create a distinctive metallic trilling sound that can be heard from over 100 yards away, produced by air rushing through specially modified wing feathers that act like tiny wind instruments. These hardy migrants can survive freezing mountain nights by entering torpor, lowering their body temperature and heart rate dramatically to conserve energy when flowers and insects are scarce. Males are territorial defenders who perform spectacular courtship dives, plummeting from heights of 40-50 feet while their tail feathers create loud popping sounds, and they're so aggressive they'll attack much larger birds, chipmunks, and even humans who venture too close to their favorite nectar sources.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny brown dynamos are surprisingly aggressive birds who will destroy the eggs and nestlings of other cavity-nesting species, and males often build multiple 'dummy nests' filled with sticks to prevent other birds from using nearby nest sites. They're prolific singers whose bubbling, cascading songs can contain over 100 notes and last up to 10 seconds, with males singing almost continuously during breeding season from dawn to dusk to defend their territories. These adaptable nesters will use almost any cavity they can find, from traditional nest boxes to old boots, mailboxes, and even the pockets of clothes left hanging on clotheslines. They're remarkable migrants who travel thousands of miles between their breeding grounds in North America and wintering areas in Central and South America, with some individuals making round trips of over 6,000 miles despite weighing only about as much as two quarters.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These vocal owls are famous for their distinctive hooting call that sounds like 'Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?' and they're one of the few owl species that regularly calls during daylight hours, especially on cloudy days. They're expanding their range westward from their traditional eastern North American habitat, now establishing populations in the Pacific Northwest where they compete with the closely related Spotted Owl for territory and resources. These versatile hunters have an unusually varied diet for owls, catching everything from mice and birds to frogs, fish, crayfish, and even large insects, and they're skilled waders who will stand in shallow water to catch aquatic prey. They're surprisingly aggressive defenders of their territory and have been known to attack humans who venture too close to their nests, diving at intruders with their sharp talons while giving harsh alarm calls.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These plain-looking birds are among the most persistent singers in North America, with males delivering their flowing, warbling songs almost continuously from dawn to dusk throughout the breeding season, sometimes singing over 3,000 songs per day. They're master nest builders who construct hanging cup nests suspended from forked branches, weaving together plant fibers, spider webs, and other materials so skillfully that the nests can survive strong winds and storms. These long-distance migrants travel from their breeding grounds across North America to wintering areas in Central America and northern South America, navigating thousands of miles using celestial cues and magnetic fields. They're surprisingly difficult to spot despite being common, as their drab gray-green plumage provides perfect camouflage among the leaves where they forage for insects, and they move deliberately through the canopy rather than flitting about like warblers.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These small flycatchers are part of the notoriously difficult-to-identify Empidonax group, but they give themselves away with their distinctive 'se-lip' call that sounds like a sharp hiccup, quite different from their look-alike relatives. They're high-elevation specialists who prefer mature coniferous forests, particularly those with Douglas fir and other tall conifers, and they're indicators of healthy old-growth forest ecosystems. These patient hunters typically perch on dead branches in the forest canopy, making short flights to catch flying insects before returning to the same or nearby perch, and they're known for their habit of flicking their wings and tail nervously while perched. Named after William Hammond, a 19th-century army surgeon and naturalist, they're long-distance migrants who winter in the mountains of Central America, traveling thousands of miles between their breeding and wintering grounds despite weighing only about as much as three pennies.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These mountain finches are nomadic wanderers whose movements are largely unpredictable, appearing in large numbers in some areas one year and being completely absent the next, following the availability of conifer seeds across the western mountains. They're accomplished singers with complex, warbling songs that can last up to 30 seconds and include imitations of other bird species, making them among the most musical of the finches. These high-altitude specialists have longer wings than their House Finch relatives, an adaptation for their nomadic lifestyle that requires long-distance flights between mountain ranges in search of food. Named after ornithologist John Cassin, males are distinguished from similar Purple Finches by their bright red crown that contrasts sharply with their brown nape, while females are heavily streaked and can be challenging to distinguish from female Purple and House Finches without careful observation.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These ancient birds are living dinosaurs whose fossil record extends back 2.5 million years, making them one of the oldest bird species still alive today, and their distinctive trumpeting calls can be heard from over two miles away. They're devoted partners who mate for life and perform elaborate dancing displays involving leaping, bowing, and tossing sticks and grass into the air, with these dances serving to strengthen pair bonds and occurring throughout the year, not just during breeding season. These impressive migrants form some of the most spectacular wildlife gatherings in North America, with over 500,000 birds funneling through Nebraska's Platte River valley each spring in one of the continent's greatest migration spectacles. They're surprisingly intelligent birds who teach their young migration routes and feeding techniques, and families stay together for nearly a year, with the young learning essential survival skills from their parents during their first migration south.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These hardy ground-dwellers are among the most widely distributed songbirds in the world, found across North America, Europe, Asia, and even North Africa, with over 40 recognized subspecies adapted to different climates and habitats. They're perfectly adapted for life in open country, with their earth-toned plumage providing excellent camouflage against bare soil, and they have the unusual habit of using their bills to excavate shallow depressions in the ground for dust bathing. These early nesters can begin breeding while snow is still on the ground, and they're one of the few songbirds that regularly walk rather than hop, moving across the ground with a distinctive gait while searching for seeds and insects. Males perform spectacular flight displays during breeding season, climbing high into the sky while singing before diving earthward with wings folded, and their distinctive black 'horns' (actually elongated feathers) can be raised or lowered depending on their mood.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These desert specialists are master architects who build elaborate stone pathways leading to their nest entrances, carefully selecting and arranging hundreds of small pebbles, bone fragments, and other objects to create decorative walkways that can extend several feet from the nest. They're incredibly agile climbers who can scale vertical rock faces with ease, using their long, slightly curved bills to probe deep crevices for insects and spiders that other birds can't reach. These vocal performers have one of the largest song repertoires of any North American bird, with males capable of singing over 100 different song types, and they often incorporate sounds from their environment, including mechanical noises, into their complex vocalizations. They're perfectly camouflaged for their rocky habitat, with gray-brown plumage that matches the color of weathered stone so precisely that they seem to disappear when they freeze against a rock face.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These colorful little falcons are North America's smallest raptor and the only kestrel found in the Americas, with males sporting blue-gray wings and rusty backs while females are more uniformly rusty-brown with dark barring. They're unique among raptors for their ability to see ultraviolet light, which helps them track small mammals by following the UV-reflective urine trails that voles and mice leave as they move through grass. These cavity nesters readily use nest boxes and have benefited from nest box programs, though their populations have declined significantly in recent decades due to habitat loss and pesticide use. They're accomplished hunters who can hover in place like tiny helicopters while scanning for prey, and they have the unusual habit of pumping their tails up and down when perched, a behavior that may help them maintain balance or communicate with other kestrels.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These unusual ducks were once called 'Baldpates' because of the distinctive white crown stripe that makes males look like they're wearing tiny white caps, and they're the only dabbling ducks that regularly graze on land like geese. They're notorious food pirates who spend more time on deep water than other marsh ducks, stealing food from diving ducks and coots when they surface with their hard-earned meals. These versatile foragers have goose-like bills that are perfectly adapted for both grazing on grass shoots and aquatic vegetation, making them equally at home on golf courses and wetlands. They're late nesters who often don't begin breeding until other dabblers have finished, and males perform elaborate courtship displays where they extend their necks low while raising their wing tips to flash brilliant white wing patches.

These spectacular migrants create living snow storms when massive flocks swirl down from the sky amid a cacophony of honking, sometimes covering entire fields in a blanket of white and black feathers. They come in two color morphs controlled by a single gene—the classic white form and the 'Blue Goose' with dark body and white head, and their genetics work like a simple dominant-recessive trait. These speed-eating machines have incredibly fast digestion, processing food in just 1-2 hours and producing 6-15 droppings per hour, especially when grubbing for muddy rhizomes. They're marathon walkers whose goslings can trek up to 50 miles with their parents in the first three weeks of life, traveling from nest sites to better brood-rearing areas across the Arctic tundra.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These submarine specialists have solid bones instead of hollow ones like most birds, making them less buoyant and perfectly designed for underwater fishing expeditions where they can dive up to 200 feet deep. They're living torpedoes who need a runway like airplanes, requiring 30 yards to a quarter-mile of open water to run across the surface while flapping before they can achieve takeoff speeds of over 70 mph. These devoted parents and their two chicks can consume an astounding half-ton of fish over a 15-week breeding period, with adults swallowing most prey underwater using sharp, backward-pointing projections in their mouths to grip slippery fish. They're the ultimate helicopter parents in reverse—adults abandon their 12-week-old juveniles to migrate south first, leaving the young to form flocks and figure out their own migration routes weeks later.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These California endemics are North America's most sedentary birds, rarely traveling more than 1,300 feet from where they were born and spending their entire lives in the same patch of chaparral. They're famous for their distinctive 'bouncing-ball' song that sounds like a ping-pong ball dropped on a table, accelerating as it settles, and they sing this mechanical trill all year long from deep within dense shrubs. These devoted partners may pair up when they're only 30-40 days old and stay with that same mate for their entire lives, with both parents sharing incubation duties in shifts. Despite having 'wren' in their name, they're not wrens at all but are actually members of the parrotbill family, making them the only North American representative of a bird family otherwise found exclusively in Asia.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These ancient desert dwellers have been living in North America for at least 400,000 years, with fossils found across the southwestern United States dating back to the late Pleistocene era. Named after Thomas Say, the 'father of American entomology,' by Napoleon's nephew Charles Bonaparte in 1819, they're the northernmost-breeding flycatcher in the world, extending their range all the way to the Arctic tundra. These resourceful nesters are ultimate recyclers who will use old nests built by robins, swallows, and other phoebes, and they're so attached to good nesting sites that one pair in Kansas used the same nest for five consecutive years. They're fearless urban adapters who nest in the most unusual places including mailboxes, machinery, and even on the Alaska pipeline, potentially following it even farther north than any other flycatcher has ever bred.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These regal giants are the world's largest terns, wielding brilliant red 'fish-knife' bills that make them unmistakable among their smaller relatives, and they're so aggressive in defending their colonies that they'll chase predatory birds and even attack humans who venture too close. They're devoted parents who continue feeding their young for months after fledging, even following them to wintering grounds to ensure the juveniles master the difficult art of fishing. The world's largest breeding colony exists on a small artificial island in the Columbia River between Oregon and Washington, where over 6,000 pairs gather each year in one of North America's most spectacular seabird spectacles. These remarkably long-lived birds can reach at least 32 years old, with an average lifespan of 12 years, and they're truly cosmopolitan species found on every continent except Antarctica, earning their name from early ornithologists who associated them with the Caspian Sea.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These spectacular Asian immigrants arrived in North America in the 1880s and quickly became one of the continent's most popular game birds, with males sporting iridescent copper-and-gold plumage and rooster-like crowing that can be heard from up to a mile away. They're equipped with specialized breast muscles that deliver explosive bursts of power, allowing them to flush nearly vertically into the air and reach speeds of nearly 40 miles per hour, with one record-breaking individual flying four miles across a body of water in strong winds. These hardy survivors can cope with extreme cold by simply remaining dormant for days at a time, and they practice 'harem-defense polygyny' where one male jealously guards a small group of females during breeding season. They're notorious nest pirates who sometimes lay eggs in other ground-nesting birds' nests and may even harass species like Gray Partridges and Greater Prairie-Chickens, with some males becoming so confused by cross-species imprinting that they chase away male prairie-chickens while courting the females.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These 'whistlers' earned their nickname from hunters who recognized the distinctive whistling sound their wings make in flight, especially pronounced in cold weather, and they're famous for their dramatic courtship displays with up to 14 different moves including the spectacular 'head throw kick' where males bend their heads back to touch their rumps before thrusting forward and kicking up water. Their chicks are true daredevils who leap from nest cavities up to 40 feet high just one day after hatching, tumbling to the ground as their mothers call from below, and they undergo a remarkable eye color transformation from gray-brown at hatching through purple-blue, blue, and green-blue before finally achieving the brilliant yellow that gives them their name. These cavity nesters are notorious for their communal egg-laying habits, with females often depositing eggs in other goldeneyes' nests, Wood Duck boxes, and even Hooded Merganser nests, creating mixed broods called 'creches' when territorial fights scatter ducklings between different mothers. The oldest known individual lived at least 20 years and 5 months, proving these hardy diving ducks are built for the long haul in North America's northern waters.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These fearless tyrants live up to their scientific name 'Tyrannus tyrannus' (meaning 'tyrant of tyrants') by aggressively attacking much larger predators like hawks, crows, and squirrels, and they've been known to knock unsuspecting Blue Jays right out of trees with their dive-bombing tactics. They're birds with split personalities who maintain strict breeding territories and eat only flying insects during summer, but completely transform into peaceful fruit-eating flock birds when they migrate to South American forests for winter. These business-suited birds sport a hidden crown of yellow, orange, or red feathers that they reveal only when facing threats, simultaneously stretching their beaks wide to show a bright red gape while dive-bombing intruders. They're devoted parents who feed their young for an unusually long seven weeks, which limits them to raising just one brood per season, and both adults and nestlings regularly regurgitate pellets of insect exoskeletons as a byproduct of their insectivorous lifestyle.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These cerulean jewels of the western mountains are unique among thrushes for their kestrel-like hunting style, hovering in mid-air with long wings before making quick dives to snatch insects, and they're surprisingly practical when it comes to romance—females choose mates based solely on the quality of nesting cavities offered, completely ignoring male singing ability, flying skills, or good looks. They're fierce competitors who arrive early at nesting grounds to claim the best tree cavities before Tree Swallows can steal them, and they've adapted so well to human-provided nest boxes that most of our knowledge about them comes from studying these artificial homes rather than natural sites. These devoted partners engage in charming feeding rituals where males bring food to incubating females, who may beg fledgling-style with open beaks and quivering wings, or more subtly signal their hunger by flicking the wing farthest from their mate. They're remarkably long-lived for small songbirds, with the oldest recorded individual reaching at least 9 years old, and they've become so dependent on nest boxes that many now breed in more open areas than their ancestors ever inhabited.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny but ferocious hunters are no bigger than House Sparrows yet regularly take prey up to three times their own size, including Northern Bobwhites, Northern Flickers, and even chickens, making them the David among Goliaths of the owl world. Unlike most owls, they lack the asymmetrical ears and facial discs that enhance hearing, instead relying on their piercing yellow eyes and daytime hunting habits to surprise unsuspecting songbirds. They're master illusionists with a pair of false 'eyes' on the back of their necks that may fool attackers into thinking they're being watched, and when truly threatened, they raise tufts on the sides of their heads like tiny horned demons. These clever cache-builders store extra food in tree cavities or hang prey on thorns like miniature shrikes, and they're so notorious among songbirds that chickadees, wrens, and other small birds will mob them relentlessly—a behavior that often helps birdwatchers locate these otherwise unobtrusive owls.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These quintessential 'seagulls' are the intelligent, adaptable, and cunning opportunists of the bird world, recently split from their European cousins in 2024 to become the American Herring Gull, and they're equipped with special salt glands above their eyes that allow them to drink seawater by excreting excess salt through their nostrils. They're devoted but demanding parents who feed their chicks day and night for up to 12 weeks, with each parent offering up to half a pound of food per day to near-fledging young, though the third chick in a clutch often struggles as the smallest and last to hatch. These remarkable survivors can live at least 29 years, making them among the longest-lived gulls, and they've mastered the art of thermoregulation by panting to cool off and orienting their bodies to keep dark plumage out of direct sunlight while incubating. They're expanding their range southward along the Atlantic Coast, potentially displacing Laughing Gulls, while simultaneously being pushed out of northern areas by the larger Great Black-backed Gulls, creating a complex dance of gull territorial shifts across North America.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These lapis-blue jewels are unique among songbirds for their unusual molting strategy—they begin replacing feathers after breeding, then migrate to southwestern 'molting hotspots' where monsoon rains provide abundant insects, and finish their molt before continuing south for winter. They're musical innovators whose young males arrive on breeding grounds without songs of their own, then create unique lifelong compositions by rearranging syllables and combining fragments from several older males in their neighborhood. These social learners form 'song neighborhoods' where males from the same area develop similar songs and learn to recognize and tolerate each other, responding more aggressively to unfamiliar songs from outsiders. Named 'Passerina amoena' meaning 'beautiful sparrow' by early naturalists who were captivated by their stunning appearance, they can live at least 9 years and have been lighting up western brushlands with their squeaky, jumbled territorial songs for generations.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These Arctic survivors are among the world's most cold-adapted birds, capable of surviving temperatures down to -65°F by growing 31% more plumage by weight in winter and tunneling into snow for overnight shelter in foot-long burrows. In 2024, ornithologists unified Common, Hoary, and Lesser Redpolls into a single species after discovering they're nearly genetically identical, with visible differences controlled by just one chromosomal inversion or 'supergene.' They're remarkably intelligent birds that pass string-pulling tests with ease and have been observed shaking seeds from birch catkins then dropping to the ground to collect them from the flat snow surface. These nomadic wanderers breed around the Arctic Ocean in numbers estimated in the hundreds of millions, and some individuals are incredibly far-ranging—with banding records showing birds traveling from Michigan to Siberia, Alaska to the eastern U.S., and Belgium to China.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These specialized finches are living puzzles of evolution, with their crossed bill tips perfectly designed to pry open tightly closed conifer cones by placing the bill under a scale and biting down, using their stronger closing muscles to push the scale up and expose the nutritious seeds inside. They're so dependent on conifer seeds that they feed them to their young and can breed anytime they find a large cone crop, even in the depths of winter, making them one of the few North American birds that might nest in January. These nomadic wanderers exist as multiple 'types' that represent one of ornithology's greatest classification puzzles—each type has different calls, feeds on specific conifer species, and rarely interbreeds despite sometimes joining mixed flocks, suggesting they may be evolving into separate species. They're unpredictable irruptive migrants that can suddenly appear far south of their normal range when cone crops fail, bringing their sharp metallic calls and chattering flocks to unexpected places where birdwatchers eagerly await their arrival.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These familiar acrobats of the air are equipped with built-in magnetic compasses that help them navigate during migration, with chicks as young as two days old already showing preferences for magnetic bearings that would guide them in the correct direction for their fall journey. They're remarkably site-faithful birds with most individuals returning to breed at the colony where they hatched, often nesting within a few meters of the previous year's nest site, and many also return to the same wintering locations year after year. These adaptable scavengers have learned to exploit human-created food sources so effectively that when waste management practices shift from open landfills to closed incinerators, local gull populations often drop dramatically, forcing them to find new feeding grounds. They're surprisingly social nesters whose colonies sometimes include two-female couples that create 'superclutches' of 5-7 eggs when both females lay in the same nest after being fertilized by an obliging male, and they can live remarkably long lives with the oldest recorded individual reaching at least 27 years and 6 months.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These speed demons of the sky are the fastest animals on Earth, capable of reaching speeds up to 200 mph during their spectacular hunting stoops from heights over half a mile, and they're so widespread they're found on every continent except Antarctica and on many oceanic islands. They're living conservation success stories that were virtually eradicated from eastern North America by DDT poisoning in the mid-20th century but have made an incredible comeback thanks to captive breeding programs that were greatly assisted by falconers' thousand-year-old knowledge of handling these prized hunting birds. These urban adapters have successfully colonized many large cities where skyscrapers provide perfect cliff-like nesting sites and abundant prey in the form of pigeons and other city birds. They're remarkably long-lived raptors with the oldest recorded individual reaching at least 19 years and 9 months, and they maintain their reputation as one of the most prized falconry birds due to their strong hunting ability, high trainability, and versatility.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These ethereal songsters of old-growth conifer forests are living examples of evolution in action, actively hybridizing with Hermit Warblers in narrow zones in Oregon and Washington, with the more aggressive Townsend's slowly displacing their cousins as the hybrid zones gradually shift. They're sweet-toothed specialists who defend winter territories in Mexico around trees infested with scale insects, feeding extensively on the sugary 'honeydew' excretions that provide such rich energy they're worth fighting for. These perfectionist architects sometimes partially construct a nest in one tree, then dismantle it completely and move all the materials to another tree to finish building, showing remarkable flexibility in their construction standards. Named after American naturalist John Kirk Townsend who first collected a specimen at the mouth of the Columbia River in 1835 during his epic cross-continental trek with botanist Thomas Nuttall, they can live at least 10 years and 8 months, spending their time high in the canopy like tiny colorful ornaments hunting insects and larvae.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These understated pirates of the duck world are notorious food thieves who regularly snatch meals from diving ducks as they surface, and they've also been observed stealing food directly from American Coots, proving that elegance doesn't preclude larceny. They're remarkably productive mothers who lay an egg a day during their 7-12 egg clutches, requiring so much protein during this stressful period that females eat significantly more invertebrates than males and rely on nutrient reserves stored in their bodies during winter. These conservation success stories have dramatically increased in numbers since the 1980s thanks to wetland protection programs, and their smart nesting strategy of choosing islands within marshes provides natural protection from land-based predators. They're surprisingly long-lived for dabbling ducks, with the oldest recorded individual reaching at least 19 years and 6 months—a male banded in Saskatchewan in 1962 who was shot during hunting season in Louisiana in 1981, proving these 'gray ghosts' can have remarkably long lives.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These elegant Arctic nomads were first described by Lewis and Clark during their western expedition, with Meriwether Lewis dubbing them 'whistling swans' after hearing their characteristic wing-whistling calls that can be heard from great distances. They're devoted romantics who form permanent pair bonds by age 2-3 and feed and roost together year-round, embodying the ideals of romance that have made swans symbols of love for centuries. These hardy defenders breed in the remote Arctic where parents courageously face down foxes, weasels, wolves, bears, gulls, ravens, jaegers, and even Golden Eagles to protect their nests, though they wisely retreat when truly massive predators like people approach from far away. They're surprisingly long-lived birds with the oldest known individual reaching at least 23 years and 7 months, and they have an unusual sleeping pattern—preferring land during breeding season but switching to sleeping on water during winter months.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These melancholy songsters of the northern forests are renowned for their hauntingly beautiful, flute-like songs that sound like 'oh, holy holy, ah, purity purity eeh, sweetly sweetly,' and they're part of an elevation-based thrush community where Veeries live at low elevations, Hermit Thrushes at middle elevations, and Swainson's Thrushes at high elevations in northeastern mountains. They're creative nesters who have been found building homes in the most unusual places including cemetery graves, golf courses, and even mine shafts, though they typically prefer trees and shrubs in the West and ground sites in the East. These resourceful foragers use a unique 'foot quivering' technique where they shake bits of grass with their feet to startle insects into movement, and they also quiver their feet as a relaxation behavior after spotting flying predators. They're surprisingly long-lived for small songbirds, with the oldest recorded individual reaching at least 10 years and 10 months, and they make several distinct calls around their nests including kitten-like mewing sounds, 'quit quit' noises while rearranging eggs, and 'pweet pweet' morning greetings between mates.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These iridescent blackbirds are the #1 threat to corn crops in North America, causing multimillion-dollar damage by eating both ripening corn and sprouts, and they're equipped with a hard keel inside their upper mandible that works like a built-in nutcracker for sawing open acorns. They're resourceful and opportunistic foragers who follow plows to catch invertebrates, wade into water to catch fish, steal worms from robins, and even kill and eat adult birds, proving they'll eat almost anything including garbage. These intelligent birds practice 'anting' behavior where they hunker down with wings spread and let ants crawl over their bodies, using the formic acid from ant stings to rid themselves of parasites, and they've also been observed using walnut juice, citrus fruits, marigolds, and even mothballs for the same purpose. They're surprisingly long-lived with the oldest recorded individual reaching at least 23 years and 1 month, and they form massive winter roosts with other blackbird species that can number in the millions of individuals, creating some of the most spectacular bird aggregations in North America.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These remarkably adaptable hummingbirds are among the most widespread in the West, thriving everywhere from scorching deserts to mountain forests and even urban areas, making them one of the most successful hummingbird species in North America. They're living metabolic marvels whose hearts beat an average of 480 times per minute at rest, but during cold nights they enter torpor and their heart rate drops dramatically to just 45-180 beats per minute while breathing becomes sporadic to conserve energy. These precision feeders have grooved tongues that work like tiny pumps, extending through their nearly closed bills at 13-17 licks per second to consume an average of 0.61 milliliters per meal, and in cold weather they can eat three times their body weight in nectar daily. They're surprisingly long-lived for such tiny birds, with the oldest known individual reaching at least 11 years and 2 months, and their coffee bean-sized eggs are incubated in expandable nests made of plant down and spider silk that grow larger as the babies develop.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These spectacular 'miniature dinosaurs' are one of only two domesticated birds native to the New World (along with Muscovy Ducks), and they have an exceptional fossil record dating back over 5 million years thanks to their large size and compact bones. They're remarkable comeback stories who were nearly extinct in the early 1900s but have recovered so successfully through wildlife management that they now occur in every state except Alaska, achieved through the 1940s discovery that only wild-caught birds (not farm turkeys) could survive reintroduction to the wild. These surprisingly athletic birds are excellent swimmers who tuck their wings close, spread their tails, and kick to propel themselves through water, and despite their bulk they can fly powerfully into treetop roosts at the end of each day. They're ancient American treasures whose English name may derive from early shipping routes that passed through the country of Turkey on their way to European markets, and their rich taste from eating wild nuts made them so popular in Europe that English colonists brought domesticated turkeys back to America—completing a remarkable round-trip journey for this iconic species.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These magnificent giants are North America's heaviest flying birds, with males averaging over 26 pounds and requiring a 100-meter 'runway' of open water for takeoff, running hard across the surface with sounds like galloping horses to generate enough speed to become airborne. They're remarkable conservation success stories who were nearly extinct by the late 1800s due to market hunting for their feathers (used for fashionable hats and powder puffs) and flight feathers (coveted for writing quills), but aggressive conservation efforts helped them recover by the early 2000s. These devoted partners form pair bonds at 3-4 years old and are assumed to mate for life, staying together year-round and using an unusual incubation method where they warm their eggs by covering them with their webbed feet rather than just sitting on them. They're surprisingly mobile on land despite their awkward appearance, capable of walking more than a mile at a time even when traveling with cygnets less than a week old, and they can live remarkably long lives with the oldest known individual reaching at least 26 years and 2 months in the wild.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These Eurasian immigrants are the 'devil birds' of western North America, earning their nickname from frustrated hunters who chase them up steep rocky terrain where they run and scamper with the agility and speed of mountain goats, their namesake calls echoing across dry slopes. They're resourceful water-seekers who live in some of the driest country on the continent, taking advantage of any water source from rivers to barely moist seeps, and during hot summer months they'll even venture 10 feet underground into mineshafts just for a drink. These meticulous groomers bathe in dust on an almost daily basis, making shallow depressions in the ground and tossing dirt over their bodies to keep their feathers in perfect condition. They're birds of international distinction, serving as the national bird of both Pakistan and Iraq, and they've successfully established populations not only across western North America but also in Hawaii and New Zealand, proving their remarkable adaptability to diverse arid environments.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These small but fierce 'lady hawks' were the favored hunting companions of medieval noblewomen including Catherine the Great and Mary Queen of Scots, who used them to hunt Sky Larks, and their name comes from 'esmerillon,' the old French term for the species. They're clever cooperative hunters who have been observed working in pairs to take down large flocks of waxwings—one Merlin attacks from below to flush the flock while the other swoops in moments later to capitalize on the confusion. These resourceful nesters don't build their own homes but instead take over old nests from other raptors, crows, or magpies, sometimes even laying their eggs right on top of a magpie nest's dome rather than inside the cavity. They're remarkable recovery stories who bounced back from twentieth-century DDT-related declines and have adapted so well to urban life that they're increasingly common around towns where House Sparrows provide a steady food supply, and the oldest known individual lived at least 11 years and 11 months, traveling from New York to New Brunswick during his long life.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These remarkable memory champions bury tens of thousands of seeds each summer and remember the locations of most of them, using a special pouch under their tongue to carry seeds long distances and creating the foundation for entire pine forests through their forgotten caches. They're unusual among the crow family because males develop brood patches and take turns incubating eggs alongside females, allowing them to breed as early as January or February in harsh mountain conditions by feeding their nestlings from stored seed caches rather than fresh food. These discerning gourmets test seeds for quality by 'bill clicking'—rapidly opening and closing their bills while moving seeds up and down—and they choose the best Colorado pinyon seeds by color, refusing all but the darkest brown ones. They were one of only three new bird species discovered during the Lewis and Clark expedition, first spotted by Captain William Clark in August 1805 who mistook this crow family member for a woodpecker, and they feast on whitebark pine seeds that contain more calories per ounce than chocolate.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These unassuming aerial acrobats have one of the most unique wing structures in the bird world—minuscule hooks on the leading edges of their primary feathers that feel like touching a rough file when you run your finger from base to tip, earning them both their common name and their scientific names 'Stelgidopteryx' (scraper wing) and 'serripennis' (saw feather). They're exceptional fliers who accomplish something most birds cannot—molting some of their feathers while still in flight, taking around 100 days to completely grow new plumage while maintaining their aerial lifestyle. These adaptable nesters are opportunists who don't excavate their own burrows but instead take advantage of holes created by other birds and mammals, and they're remarkably flexible in choosing nesting sites from natural riverbanks to human-made structures. They're the solitary swallows of their family, preferring to nest individually rather than in the large colonies favored by Bank Swallows, and they fly with distinctively slower and more deliberate wingbeats than their relatives, often skimming lower over water surfaces as they hunt for insects.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These ghostly silent hunters are living sound laboratories with the best hearing of any animal ever tested—they can catch mice in complete darkness using sound alone, even when prey is hidden under a foot of snow or thick vegetation. They're remarkable digestive recyclers who swallow their prey whole (skin, bones, and all) then cough up pellets twice daily instead of passing all that material through their digestive tract, creating perfect records of their diet that scientists study to understand entire ecosystems. These recently reclassified birds were split in 2024 from the worldwide 'Barn Owl' into three distinct species—American Barn Owl (Americas), Eastern Barn Owl (South Asia to Australia), and Western Barn Owl (Europe, Africa, western Asia)—ending the reign of what was once considered the most widespread land bird on Earth. They're surprisingly long-lived nocturnal predators with the oldest known individual reaching at least 15 years and 5 months in Ohio, and their heart-shaped facial discs work like satellite dishes to funnel even the faintest sounds directly to their asymmetrically placed ears for pinpoint prey location.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These striking monochrome warblers are living examples of cultural ornithology—the Chinook tribe of the Pacific Northwest knew them long before European naturalists arrived and called them 'Ah Kah a qual,' while John Kirk Townsend didn't formally describe the species until 1837 near Portland, Oregon. They're remarkably fearless birds who hop boldly through the lower and middle levels of coniferous forests, seemingly without concern for nearby humans, making them one of the more approachable warbler species for birdwatchers. These short- to medium-distance migrants follow mountain ranges and the Pacific coastline southward to Mexico, but despite these natural landmarks, some individuals get confused and turn up every year in eastern states far from their normal range. They're minimalist beauties who wear only the tiniest spot of yellow—just above and in front of the eye—while the rest of their plumage consists entirely of bold black, white, and gray patterns that create one of the most striking yet simple color schemes in the warbler family.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These remarkable navigators can find their way home even when released from distant locations while blindfolded, using an incredible combination of magnetic field sensing, sound, smell, and sun position cues that made them invaluable message carriers for the U.S. Army Signal Corps during both World Wars. They're ancient companions of humanity with a relationship so old that Mesopotamian cuneiform tablets and Egyptian hieroglyphics document their domestication over 5,000 years ago, making it impossible to determine their original wild range. These living laboratories of evolution fascinated Charles Darwin, who kept pigeons for years after his Beagle voyage and used observations of their incredible breed diversity—from wild birds to fantastically modified domestic varieties—to help formulate aspects of his theory of evolution. They're surprisingly long-lived urban survivors with one retired Army Signal Corps bird named Levi reaching 31 years old, though feral city pigeons average only 2.4 years due to urban hazards, and they display remarkable color variation including blue-bar, red-bar, checker, spread, pied, and solid red or white forms that people have named and recognized for centuries.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These brilliant buttery songsters are master architects who respond to Brown-headed Cowbird nest parasitism by building new nests directly on top of the parasitized ones, sometimes creating remarkable six-tiered apartment buildings that demonstrate their determination to raise their own young. They're part of a diverse international family with several resident forms found in Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean where males can sport chestnut caps or even entire chestnut heads, making the North American migratory form just one variation of this widespread species. These sweet singers are occasionally victims of their own curiosity, with individuals sometimes found caught in the sticky strands of orb weaver spider webs—a dangerous hazard for such small birds navigating through dense vegetation. They're surprisingly long-lived for such tiny creatures, with the oldest known individual being a female who reached at least 11 years old when recaptured during banding operations in New York, and their tumbling whistled song that sounds like 'sweet sweet sweet I'm so sweet' makes them one of the most commonly heard warblers across North America.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These nomadic fruit connoisseurs are living GPS systems for berries, possessing an uncanny ability to find fruit nearly everywhere—flocks sometimes appear in desert areas, locate an isolated shrub, devour its fruit in minutes, and vanish like feathered phantoms. They're remarkable wanderers whose movements can be truly epic, with one individual banded in British Columbia recovered 13 months later in South Dakota, and another flying 280 miles in just 11 days during their restless search for food. These regal vagabonds are part of an exclusive club—only three waxwing species exist worldwide: Bohemian (North America and Eurasia), Cedar (North America), and Japanese (eastern Asia)—and unlike most songbirds, they don't hold territories or sing true songs, instead communicating with high-pitched trills as they roam in large groups. They're living mood rings whose waxy wing tips and tail bands change color based on the carotenoid pigments in the fruit they eat, with the waxy tips growing larger as the birds age, creating a beautiful record of their dietary adventures and life experience.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These flashy-legged 'marshpipers' are the noisy tattletales of the wetlands, earning colloquial names like telltale, tattler, and yelper for their strident alarm calls that alert every creature within earshot to potential danger. They're paradoxical birds who are both familiar and mysterious—despite their widespread range and recognizable appearance, they're one of the least-studied shorebirds on the continent because they nest in mosquito-ridden bogs deep in the North American boreal forests. These adaptable waders are the deep-water specialists of their family, preferring to wade in deeper water than other sandpipers and earning their 'marshpiper' nickname for this distinctive behavior that sets them apart from their shallow-water relatives. They're surprisingly arboreal for shorebirds, often perching atop trees on their breeding grounds to watch for nest predators—an unusual behavior that showcases their versatility beyond the typical mudflat stereotype of their family.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These master mimics are the perfect beginner's bird call to learn—once you've heard their distinctive catty mew, you'll never forget it, and they belong to the family Mimidae alongside mockingbirds and thrashers, sharing their incredible vocal abilities to copy other species' sounds. They're marathon singers whose elaborate songs can last up to 10 minutes, with males using loud territorial proclamations and softer intimate versions near the nest, while females sometimes sing the quiet song back to their mates in a charming duet. These aptly named skulkers belong to the genus 'Dumetella,' which means 'small thicket,' perfectly describing where you should look for these secretive birds who love dense, tangled vegetation and vine-covered areas. They're surprisingly long-lived for such small songbirds, with the oldest known individual reaching at least 17 years and 11 months when recaptured in New Jersey in 2001—a bird that had been originally banded in Maryland back in 1984, proving these gray ghosts can have remarkably long lives.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These unobtrusive little songbirds are the ultimate identification challenge for birders, so similar to Hammond's Flycatcher that even their voices—usually the most reliable character for distinguishing Empidonax flycatchers—are nearly identical, forcing experts to rely on subtle 'primary projection' differences where Dusky's wing feather tips are shorter and stubbier. They're paradoxical beneficiaries of habitat disturbance, being one of the few songbird species that may actually benefit from certain types of logging as their preferred shrubby breeding habitat increases, though this also makes them more vulnerable to Brown-headed Cowbird parasitism. These low-flying insect hunters stay fairly close to the vegetation rather than using high exposed perches, frequently giving their distinctive short, sharp 'wit' call as they forage through open coniferous woodlands, aspen groves, and streamside thickets. They're surprisingly long-lived for such small flycatchers, with the oldest recorded individual being a female who reached at least 8 years and 2 months when recaptured during banding operations in California, proving these modest birds can have substantial lifespans.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These precision-flying jewels are eastern North America's sole breeding hummingbird, occupying the largest breeding range of any North American hummingbird species, and they accomplish one of the most remarkable feats in the bird world by flying solo across the 500-mile Gulf of Mexico during migration. They're living helicopters with wings that beat about 53 times per second, but their extremely short legs prevent them from walking or hopping—the best they can do is shuffle along a perch, and they must raise their foot up and over their wing to scratch their head and neck. These adaptable nesters have become so accustomed to human habitation that they've been known to build their tiny nests on loops of chain, wire, and extension cords, showing remarkable flexibility in their construction site choices. They're surprisingly long-lived for such tiny creatures, with the oldest known individual being a female who reached at least 9 years and 2 months when recaptured in West Virginia in 2014, and males are notorious for their brief romantic commitments—staying together with females just long enough for courtship and mating before departing on their own, sometimes beginning migration as early as August.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These forest hawks have a complex relationship with American Crows that goes beyond simple mobbing—they may chase each other, steal food from one another, and even join forces to attack Great Horned Owls, though the hawk occasionally turns the tables by eating young owls while being chased by the adult. They're remarkably territorial birds who return to the same nesting territory year after year, with one individual in southern California occupying the same territory for 16 consecutive years, showing incredible site fidelity. These efficient parents teach their nestlings proper bathroom etiquette—by five days old, young Red-shouldered Hawks can shoot their feces over the edge of their nest, and bird poop on the ground below is a reliable sign of an active nest above. They're surprisingly long-lived raptors with the oldest known individual being a female who reached at least 25 years and 10 months when recaptured in California in 2000—a bird that had been originally banded in the same state back in 1974, demonstrating the remarkable longevity possible in these forest-dwelling hunters.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These buzzing songsters of the northern prairies are still the most numerous songbird of shrub communities in their range, though their distinctive dry series of short buzzes has been slowly declining for several decades according to breeding bird surveys. They're unusual among sparrows for their commuter lifestyle—unlike most species, they forage away from their breeding territories, using different areas for breeding and feeding, which allows them to have the smallest breeding territory of any Spizella sparrow species. These early-departure specialists have young that leave the nest before they can fly, hopping to the ground and running an average of 40 feet to seek cover in thickets where parents continue feeding them for another 6-8 days until their first flight. They're birds with commitment issues when it comes to relationships—while males are generally loyal to their territory year after year, females typically choose different breeding areas each season, making mated pairs that persist over subsequent years quite rare, and they're such neat housekeepers that they remove eggshells after hatching, usually carrying them away but sometimes eating them to keep the nest clean.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These ghostly nocturnal fishers are the most widespread heron in the world, and scientists find them remarkably easy to study because nestlings often disgorge their stomach contents when approached—a smelly but informative research method that reveals their diverse diet. They're indiscriminate foster parents who will brood any chick placed in their nest, apparently unable to distinguish between their own offspring and nestlings from other parents, making them the ultimate adoptive bird family. These social nesters breed in mixed-species colonies with other herons, egrets, and ibises, and their young have an unusual development pattern—leaving the nest at one month old but unable to fly until six weeks, spending their time moving through vegetation on foot and joining nighttime foraging flocks. They're surprisingly long-lived birds with the oldest known individual being a female who reached at least 21 years and 5 months when found in California in 2012, and their evening flights to feeding grounds were beautifully captured by Arthur Bent who described hearing their 'loud, choking squawk' and seeing their 'stocky form, dimly outlined against the gray sky' as they wing their way to distant marshes.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny powerhouses are the speed demons of the breeding world, accomplishing everything from finding a mate to raising independent young in just 58 days, and they only spend about 64 days total in their summer homes before heading back to Central America. They're fearless fighters who don't let their small size stop them from chasing birds as large as Blue Jays away from their territories, and they sing their distinctive 'che-bec' calls incessantly during breeding season to establish their presence. These efficient travelers cover 60-72 miles per day during their 25-day journey to wintering grounds, but unlike many songbirds who molt on breeding grounds, they wait until arriving in Mexico and Central America in mid-August to start growing new feathers. They're creative nest decorators with one documented case of a pair using dragonfly wings as nest lining, and despite their common status, they've lost more than half their population since 1970, making them a conservation concern despite their bold personalities.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These subtly handsome songbirds honor John Cassin, a nineteenth-century ornithologist who published the first major book on western U.S. birds and has multiple species named after him including Cassin's Auklet, Kingbird, Sparrow, Finch, and even a 17-year periodical cicada. They're the middle child of the former 'Solitary Vireo' complex, split in 1997 into three species, with Cassin's being intermediate in both appearance and song between the brightly colored Blue-headed Vireo and the duller gray Plumbeous Vireo. These loud complainers have a distinctive scolding call that naturalist William Dawson memorably described in 1923 as a 'rasping, nerve-grating war-cry' that makes them fairly conspicuous within their dry, open forest habitats. They're social foragers who often join mixed-species flocks of woodland birds outside the breeding season and are readily attracted to pishing sounds, making them relatively easy to spot as they forage slowly through the lower and middle parts of trees.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These elegant speed demons are the eager beavers of the duck world, starting to nest as soon as ice begins to thaw and arriving by late April in places as far north as the Northwest Territories, Canada, showing remarkable urgency in their breeding schedule. They're impressive long-distance fliers who migrate at night at speeds around 48 miles per hour, with the longest recorded nonstop flight being an astounding 1,800 miles, earning them the nickname 'greyhounds of the air.' These cosmopolitan ducks aren't restricted to North America—they also occur across Europe, the Middle East, India, and Asia, making them one of the most widely distributed duck species in the world, while their South American cousins, the White-cheeked and Yellow-billed Pintails, fill similar ecological niches. They're surprisingly long-lived waterfowl with the oldest recorded individual being a male who reached at least 22 years and 3 months when shot in Saskatchewan, Canada in 1994, demonstrating remarkable longevity for a species that faces significant hunting pressure.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These pugnacious little architects live secret lives under the cover of reeds where males routinely mate with two or more females and build at least six dummy nests for every female they mate with, with one overachiever constructing 22 nests on his territory. They're tiny but fierce warriors who fight for resources and regularly pierce eggs and kill nestlings of other Marsh Wrens and marsh-nesting birds, showing no mercy in their competitive wetland world. These boisterous songsters are the night owls of the marsh, singing not only at dawn and dusk but sometimes throughout the entire night with their rapid-fire gurgling, trilling, and buzzy songs echoing through the cattails. They're potentially two species masquerading as one—eastern and western populations show slight differences in appearance but large differences in song, with western birds being paler, drabber, and singing less musical songs, suggesting they may actually be separate species entirely.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These variable leaf-kickers are one of our most polymorphic birds, with four main groups ranging from foxy red to gray to dark brown, and they're typically seen sending up sprays of leaf litter as they scratch around in dense thickets searching for food. They're inspiring songsters whose rich melodies captivated nineteenth-century naturalist William Brewster in the Gulf of Saint Lawrence, who wrote that their voice 'rises among the evergreen woods filling the air with quivering, delicious melody, which at length dies softly, mingling with the soughing of the wind in the spruces.' These remarkable vagrants have been spotted as far away as Greenland, Iceland, Ireland, Germany, and Italy, with some probably making part of their transatlantic journey by ship after touching down to rest on vessels far from shore. They're ancient North Americans with fossils from the Pleistocene (about 11,000 years ago) found in Pennsylvania, Virginia, and at the famous La Brea tar pits in California, proving their long history on this continent.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These majestic lightning-strike hunters may move slowly and deliberately, but they can strike like lightning to grab fish or snap up gophers, thanks to specially shaped neck vertebrae that allow them to quickly strike prey at a distance. They're surprisingly lightweight giants, weighing only 5-6 pounds despite their impressive size due to hollow bones shared by all birds, and they have specialized 'powder down' feathers on their chest that continually grow and fray, which they comb with a fringed claw to remove fish slime and oils like a washcloth. These night-vision specialists can hunt both day and night thanks to a high percentage of rod-type photoreceptors in their eyes, and along the Pacific coast they're often seen poised atop floating beds of kelp waiting for meals to swim by. They're remarkably long-lived birds with the oldest recorded individual found in Texas at least 24 years and 6 months old, and they've benefited from beaver population recovery in the northeastern U.S. and southern Canada, which has created ideal patchworks of swamps and meadows for foraging and nesting.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny speed demons are the smallest hawks in Canada and the United States, appearing in a blur of motion and often disappearing in a flurry of feathers as they pursue songbirds through dense forests with their distinctive long legs, short wings, and very long tails. They're remarkable migration spectacles with more than 11,000 individuals recorded on a single October day at Cape May Point, New Jersey, as they follow landscape features during their southward journey from Canada. These size-dimorphic raptors show extreme sexual differences where females are about a third bigger and heavier than males, allowing them to catch different-sized prey—nestlings feed first on small prey caught by their father, then switch to larger prey brought by their mother as they grow. They're cat-like hunters who use their long toes and talons to impale and hold moving prey, and they've even been known to reach into wire-mesh bird traps to grab prey with their toes, carrying their catch to stumps or low branches to pluck before eating since swallowing feathers isn't normal for them like it is for owls.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These dapper shorebirds are the ultimate role-reversal species where females practice polyandry, mating with up to four males who each care for their own clutch of eggs, with one Minnesota female laying five clutches for three different males in just six weeks. They're the most widespread breeding sandpiper in North America and famous for their characteristic teetering motion that has earned them colorful nicknames like teeter-peep, teeter-bob, jerk bird, perk bird, teeter-snipe, and tip-tail. These hormone-flipped birds have males with 10 times more testosterone than females in absolute terms, but during breeding season females experience a sevenfold testosterone increase that may account for their aggressive territory-defending behavior and overall dominance. They're remarkable sperm-storage specialists where females can store sperm for up to one month, meaning eggs laid for one male may actually be fathered by a different male from a previous mating, and their chicks begin teetering almost immediately after hatching—a mysterious behavior that speeds up when nervous but stops completely when alarmed, aggressive, or courting.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These mountain giants are the third largest grouse in North America and one of the largest in the world, with only the two sage-grouse species being larger, and they're distinguished from their close relative the Dusky Grouse by their displays, plumages, vocalizations, and genetics. They're anatomical anomalies among birds with an unusual number of tail feathers—while most bird species have a consistent 10 tail feathers, Sooty Grouse can have anywhere from 15 to 22. These steely gray-blue males transform during courtship, revealing bright orange eye combs and yellow-orange air sacs in their necks, and unlike their Rocky Mountain cousins, they display from high perches in trees rather than on the ground. They're masters of camouflage where females are intricately patterned in brown, buff, and white to blend perfectly with their forest floor nesting sites, and their deep, rhythmic hooting calls are loud enough to carry through dense mountain forests but can be maddeningly difficult to locate.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These furtive skulkers are elegant yellow and gray gems amid green leaves, with males sporting sooty gray hoods highlighted by striking white crescents above and below their eyes, and they're known for hiding in dense undergrowth where they're much more easily heard than seen. They're birds caught in a naming controversy—John James Audubon named them for his friend and editor William MacGillivray, a Scottish naturalist, even though John Kirk Townsend had already named the species Tolmie's Warbler in honor of surgeon William Fraser Tolmie, creating a scientific name that honors one person while the common name honors another. These remarkable altitude adapters nest from near sea level all the way up to 10,000 feet in elevation, showing incredible versatility in their habitat preferences across western North America's diverse mountain landscapes. They're living proof of nature's boundary-pushing tendencies, as their ranges overlap with the closely related Mourning Warbler in a small part of British Columbia's Peace region, where the two species sometimes form hybrids in this narrow zone of contact.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These elegant rare visitors to North America are living proof of birds' incredible navigational abilities, with eastern North American sightings likely coming from Iceland (evidenced by banded birds recovered in northeastern Canada) while western birds may arrive from eastern Asia, particularly easternmost Russia. They're mythologically named ducks whose species name 'penelope' honors Odysseus's wife from Greek mythology, who was rescued by a duck after being thrown into the ocean, creating a poetic connection between ancient stories and modern ornithology. These remarkably long-lived waterfowl hold impressive longevity records, with the oldest North American individual being a male shot in California at least 10 years and 7 months old, while in Europe one banded bird reached the extraordinary age of 33 years and 7 months. They're genetic bridge-builders who occasionally hybridize with their nearest relative, the American Wigeon, producing male offspring that appear intermediate between the parent species, with gray bodies and reddish heads that blend characteristics from both continents.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These mountain specialists are taxonomic shape-shifters who were once considered the same species as Pacific-slope Flycatcher under the name 'Western Flycatcher' from 1989 to 2023, but recent research has led to their reunion as subspecies groups within a single species again, showing how scientific understanding evolves. They're habitat purists who prefer mountainous forests of mixed conifer, damp woods, and shady canyons throughout the montane regions of western North America, making them true specialists of high-elevation environments. These insectivorous Neotropical migrants are conservation beneficiaries of artificial nesting platforms, which researchers have successfully used as management tools to support their populations in areas where natural nesting sites may be limited. They're more aggressive than their Pacific-slope cousins, showing behavioral differences that helped distinguish them during their period as separate species, and they represent the inland mountain form while Pacific-slope Flycatchers occupy coastal mountain ranges from southeastern Alaska to Baja California.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These misleadingly named ground birds were christened by European settlers reminded of Eurasian Tree Sparrows back home, but they actually forage on the ground, nest on the ground, and breed primarily in scrubby areas at or above the treeline in the far North. They're living on the edge nutritionally, needing to consume about 30 percent of their body weight in food and water each day—a full day's fasting is usually a death sentence as their body temperature drops and they lose nearly a fifth of their weight in that short time. These synchronized families have remarkable hatching coordination where females lay only one egg per day (sometimes skipping days) over 4-6 eggs, yet all chicks hatch within hours of each other and may not even hatch in the order their eggs were laid. They're surprisingly light-sensitive birds whose biological rhythms don't depend on vision—blind tree sparrows in captivity show normal responses to increasing day length in late winter, including sex organ growth, proving their internal clocks work independently of sight.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These elegant conservation symbols are the living emblem of the National Audubon Society, one of North America's oldest environmental organizations founded to protect birds from being killed for their feathers after Great Egrets were hunted nearly to extinction for their plumes in the late nineteenth century. They're powerful but graceful fliers who cruise at around 25 miles per hour with just two wingbeats per second, and they occasionally swim to capture prey or hover somewhat laboriously over water to dip for fish. These fashionable breeders get even more dressed up for breeding season when a patch of skin on their face turns neon green and long plumes called 'aigrettes' grow from their backs—the very adornments that were prized for ladies' hats and nearly caused their extinction. They're colony catalysts who are often the first species to arrive at mixed-species nesting colonies, and their presence may induce nesting among other species, making them important community organizers in wetland ecosystems.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These genetically fascinating sparrows come in two distinct color forms—white-striped and tan-striped—that persist because individuals almost always mate with a bird of the opposite morph, creating a unique genetic system where males of both types prefer white-striped females while both kinds of females prefer tan-striped males. They're unlikely hybrid producers who occasionally mate with the unrelated Dark-eyed Junco despite looking nothing alike, creating grayish, dully marked offspring that resemble White-throated Sparrows with white outer tail feathers. These adaptive nesters typically build on or near the ground, but when ground nests are robbed by predators, they'll construct second attempts up to 15 feet high in conifers, showing remarkable flexibility in their nesting strategy. They're crisp-faced anatomy lessons with their black eyestripe, white crown and supercilium, yellow lores, and white throat bordered by a black malar stripe, making them excellent birds for learning facial field marks while enjoying their pretty, wavering whistle of 'Oh-sweet-canada.'
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These sociable architects build intricate gourd-shaped mud nests that cluster under horizontal overhangs, with colonies ranging from small eastern groups to massive western gatherings of up to 3,700 nests in one spot. They're information-sharing neighbors who watch each other for food-finding cues—when one swallow has trouble finding food, it will follow a successful neighbor, and during poor weather conditions, a swallow finding food may give specific calls to alert others to large insect swarms. These sneaky egg-layers practice brood parasitism within their own species, sometimes carrying their own eggs in their bills to place in another female's nest, creating complex family dynamics within the colony. They're vocal family reunification experts whose young congregate in large groups called creches after leaving their nests, with parents able to find their own chicks primarily by voice recognition, aided by the species' highly variable juvenile plumage patterns that may help with visual identification.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These champion brood parasites are perhaps the top egg-dumpers among North American ducks, laying their eggs in the nests of other Redheads as well as Mallards, Canvasbacks, Northern Pintails, Gadwalls, Northern Shovelers, Ruddy Ducks, American Wigeons, and even Northern Harriers. They're gymnastic courtship performers where males execute a spectacular 'head throw' display, bending nearly in half with their necks bent far over their backs until their heads touch their tails, then snapping forward while giving a loud, catlike 'mee-ow' call. These exceptionally gregarious 'rafting ducks' are so sociable they sometimes alight at hunting decoys before hunters have finished setting them up, and they form massive winter flocks of up to 60,000 birds in the twin Laguna Madre bays of Texas and Mexico. They're seagrass specialists during winter, with much of their population concentrating in these two Gulf of Mexico bays that share the same name, where they feed extensively on underwater vegetation in the shallow coastal waters.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These masked bandits of the marsh were among the first New World birds catalogued by science when Linnaeus described a Maryland specimen in 1766, and they're vocal skulkers whose distinctive 'witchety-witchety-witchety' songs and husky 'chuck' calls help reveal their presence in tangled vegetation. They're surprisingly vulnerable to unusual predators, with documented cases including one migrating yellowthroat eaten by a Chuck-will's-widow and another found in the stomach of a largemouth bass, showing that danger can come from unexpected directions. These secretive cheaters practice infidelity where females often mate with multiple males behind their primary mate's back, attracted by the mating calls of neighboring males despite having established pair bonds. They're clever anti-parasite strategists who've developed sophisticated defenses against Brown-headed Cowbird brood parasitism, deserting nests containing cowbird eggs or building second and even third nests on top of parasitized ones to protect their own offspring.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These misnamed owls don't actually screech but instead make an accelerating series of hollow toots—the 'screech' part of their name better suits their Eastern cousin whose primary sound is a descending whinny. They're diminutive but formidable predators who occasionally take prey bigger than their own body, including cottontail rabbits, and they've been seen collecting earthworms from rainy roads and even compost piles. These master camouflagers sometimes perch at the entrance of their roost holes during the day but remain nearly invisible by pressing their head and body feathers against the tree to blend in perfectly with the bark. They're compact hunters not much taller than a standard pair of binoculars, with a remarkably wide-ranging diet that includes everything from worms and crayfish to rats and bats, making them versatile predators of western North America's woods and deserts.
