sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These nimble canopy-gleaners are flame-orange acrobats who dangle upside down from branches while foraging and weaving their remarkable hanging nests, with males sporting a neat line through the eye and a white wing patch while females are washed in gray and orange. They're musical duet partners where both males and females sing—the male more sweetly, the female often more prolifically—creating a rich soundscape in the tall trees along rivers and streams. These genetic bridge-builders frequently hybridize with Baltimore Orioles in the Great Plains where their ranges overlap, and the two species were once lumped together as the 'Northern Oriole' before genetic research revealed they're not very closely related. They're historically named birds described by William Swainson in 1827 using material collected by English father-and-son naturalists William and William Bullock in Mexico, and they're surprisingly flexible nesters who may build outside the territory where the male advertises.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These golden-faced beacons were first described by John Kirk Townsend in 1837 from a pair collected at Fort Vancouver near the Columbia River, and their buzzy songs drift down from 80-100 feet up in Pacific Northwest mountain forests. They're sister species to Townsend's Warblers—their closest relatives—and it's estimated they became distinct species sometime in the late Pleistocene epoch that ended 11,700 years ago, though they still hybridize in narrow zones that appear to be slowly moving northward. These superspecies members are part of an exclusive club with Black-throated Green and Golden-cheeked Warblers—all black-and-gray warblers with golden-yellow faces that together form what scientists call a superspecies. They're romantic choosers where some Hermit Warbler females seem to prefer mating with Townsend's Warbler-type males, but there's no evidence of Townsend's Warbler females returning the favor by mating with Hermit Warbler males.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These gems of the northern woods are voracious seed-eating machines who can consume up to 3,000 conifer seeds each day, working through spruce treetops like animated parrots hanging upside down. They're irruptive wanderers whose movements depend entirely on cone crops, and when food fails in their normal range they can move far south, sometimes showing up in ornamental spruces in cemeteries and parks. These color-changing males undergo a fascinating molt where red feathers initially appear pink due to unpigmented barbules that mask the red, but as these barbules wear off through the seasons, brilliant red shows through for spring and summer breeding displays. They're asymmetrical specialists where individuals with lower mandibles crossing to the right are approximately three times more common than those crossing to the left, and they're opportunistic breeders who can start nesting in any of the 12 months when food is sufficient.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These historic crop-savers became legendary in 1848 when they arrived to feast on katydids (Mormon crickets) that were devouring Mormon settlers' crops in Utah, saving the harvest from complete destruction and earning a golden statue in Salt Lake City plus designation as Utah's state bird. They're opportunistic alkali fly hunters with an odd foraging strategy at salty Great Basin lakes, starting at one end of huge fly rafts and running through them with head down and bill open, snapping up flies along the way. These communicative parents have elaborate shift-change rituals when trading incubation duties, with returning mates calling to encourage reluctant partners through 'choking calls,' presenting nest material, or physically nudging them off the nest. They're aerial practice artists whose young gulls hone their midair catching skills by dropping sticks and swooping down to catch them, preparing for a lifetime of opportunistic foraging from mayflies to garbage.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These elegant water dancers perform one of the most spectacular courtship displays in the bird world, with pairs rushing across the water surface side by side in perfect synchronization during their famous 'rushing ceremony.' They're master divers who can stay underwater for up to 40 seconds while pursuing fish, using their dagger-like bills and streamlined bodies to become living torpedoes beneath the surface. These colonial nesters build floating platforms of aquatic vegetation anchored to emergent plants, and their young often ride on their parents' backs for protection during their first weeks of life. They're nearly flightless during molt when they lose all their flight feathers at once, making them temporarily vulnerable but allowing them to regrow a complete new set of feathers for the next season.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tireless songsters are among North America's most persistent singers, with males delivering up to 20,000 songs per day during breeding season, earning them the nickname 'preacher bird' for their seemingly endless musical sermons from the forest canopy. They're meticulous nest architects who build deep, cup-shaped nests suspended like hammocks between forked branches, often decorating the outside with spider webs, lichens, and bark strips for camouflage. These long-distance migrants undertake epic journeys to South America, with some individuals traveling over 5,000 miles each way, navigating by stars and magnetic fields to reach their wintering grounds in the Amazon basin. They're dedicated parents who continue feeding their fledglings for up to three weeks after they leave the nest, teaching them essential foraging skills while maintaining their territorial singing duties.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These low-flying marsh hawks are the only North American raptors that practice polygamy, with successful males sometimes mating with up to five females in a single breeding season, establishing territories that can encompass multiple nesting females. They're aerial acrobats who perform spectacular courtship displays involving dramatic dives, barrel rolls, and food transfers in midair, with males passing prey to females in graceful aerial exchanges. These ground nesters are unusual among raptors for building their nests on the ground in dense vegetation, creating platforms of sticks and grass that can be up to three feet across. They're sexually dimorphic hunters where the larger, brown females specialize in catching larger prey like ducks and rabbits, while the smaller, gray males focus on smaller prey like voles and songbirds, reducing competition between the sexes.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny mountain jewels are North America's smallest breeding bird, weighing less than a penny yet capable of incredible feats including migrations that can take them from Canada to Mexico. They're high-altitude specialists who breed in mountain meadows and forest clearings up to 11,000 feet elevation, where they've adapted to cold nights by entering torpor to conserve energy. These fearless defenders will aggressively chase away much larger birds including hawks and ravens from their territory, using their incredible speed and maneuverability as weapons. They're nectar specialists with co-evolved relationships with specific wildflowers, particularly red tubular blooms like Indian paintbrush and penstemon, and their long, needle-like bills are perfectly adapted for reaching deep into flower corollas.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These bold flycatchers are fearless defenders who will attack much larger birds including hawks, ravens, and even Great Blue Herons that venture too close to their nesting territory, using their speed and agility to drive off potential threats. They're adaptable nesters who have learned to take advantage of human infrastructure, commonly building their nests on power lines, fence posts, and building ledges, often in surprisingly urban environments. These aerial hunters perform spectacular sallying flights from prominent perches, catching insects on the wing with remarkable precision before returning to the same perch to consume their prey. They're long-distance migrants who travel from their western North American breeding grounds to wintering areas in Central America, with some individuals making stops in unexpected places like Florida during migration.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These sagebrush specialists are among the most habitat-specific birds in North America, requiring dense stands of big sagebrush for both nesting and foraging, making them excellent indicators of healthy sagebrush ecosystem conditions. They're marathon singers whose males deliver incredibly long and complex songs that can last up to 7 minutes, consisting of hundreds of notes in intricate patterns that vary geographically like regional dialects. These ground foragers are surprisingly acrobatic, often hanging upside down from sagebrush branches to reach seeds and insects, and they can run rapidly through dense brush with mouse-like agility. They're climate-sensitive migrants whose breeding success is closely tied to spring precipitation patterns that affect insect abundance, making them vulnerable to changing weather patterns in their arid western habitats.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These Arctic breeders are remarkable long-distance migrants who can fly non-stop for over 3,000 miles during migration, using fat reserves that can comprise up to 60% of their body weight as fuel for these epic journeys. They're synchronized flock performers who create mesmerizing aerial displays with thousands of individuals wheeling and turning as one, flashing their white bellies and dark backs in coordinated waves across coastal skies. These bill specialists have sensitive nerve endings in their flexible bill tips that allow them to feel for prey buried in mud and sand, probing with rapid sewing-machine-like motions to locate worms and small crustaceans. They're tidal timekeepers whose feeding schedules are precisely synchronized with tidal cycles, gathering in massive roosting flocks during high tide and dispersing to feed when mudflats are exposed.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These ground-walking tundra specialists are among the few songbirds that breed in the harsh Arctic tundra and high alpine meadows, where they nest on the ground in areas so remote that their breeding biology remained largely unknown until recent decades. They're tail-pumping walkers who rarely hop like most songbirds, instead striding across open ground with a distinctive gait while constantly pumping their tails up and down, a behavior that helps distinguish them from other small brown birds. These aerial singers perform spectacular flight displays during breeding season, climbing high into the sky while singing continuously, then parachuting down with wings and tail spread while delivering their tinkling songs. They're weather-dependent migrants whose movements are closely tied to storm systems, often appearing in large numbers at coastal and inland locations during migration when pushed by strong winds and weather fronts.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These secretive owls are masters of camouflage who can compress their bodies and raise their ear tufts to perfectly mimic broken tree branches, making them nearly invisible when roosting against tree trunks during the day. They're communal roosters who gather in groups of up to 100 individuals during winter, creating some of the largest owl roosts in North America in dense thickets and woodlots. These silent hunters have asymmetrical ear openings that allow them to pinpoint prey location with incredible precision in complete darkness, and their flight is so quiet they can approach prey without making a sound. They're nomadic wanderers whose movements are tied to rodent population cycles, appearing in large numbers during vole and mouse population peaks then disappearing when prey becomes scarce.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These high-elevation specialists are North America's largest quail and the only ones that migrate on foot, walking up and down mountainsides seasonally rather than flying, with some individuals traveling over 20 miles between summer and winter ranges. They're family-oriented birds where coveys consist of extended family groups that can include multiple generations, and they perform elaborate distraction displays when predators threaten their young, with adults feigning injury to lead threats away from chicks. These water-dependent birds require reliable water sources and will travel considerable distances daily to reach springs and streams, making them excellent indicators of healthy mountain watershed conditions. They're secretive ground-dwellers who prefer to run rather than fly when threatened, using their powerful legs to navigate steep, rocky terrain with remarkable agility, and they can virtually disappear into dense brush and rocky crevices.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These gentle giants of the finch world are remarkably tame and approachable, often allowing humans to get within arm's reach as they feed, earning them the nickname 'mope' from early naturalists who thought they seemed sluggish and stupid. They're irruptive nomads whose movements south depend entirely on cone crop failures in the boreal forest, and during invasion years they can appear in large flocks at bird feeders and ornamental trees far from their normal range. These sexually dimorphic beauties show extreme differences between males and females, with rosy-red males contrasting dramatically with golden-yellow females, and young males can take up to three years to develop their full adult plumage. They're specialized seed-crackers with powerful bills perfectly adapted for extracting seeds from tough conifer cones, and they're one of the few finches that regularly feeds their young regurgitated seeds rather than insects.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These rocky shore specialists have bright orange bills perfectly designed for prying open mussels, barnacles, and other shellfish, and they're one of the few birds that can actually open a mussel without breaking the shell. They're territorial defenders who maintain year-round territories along specific stretches of rocky coastline, with pairs often returning to the same territory for multiple breeding seasons and defending it vigorously against intruders. These tidal timekeepers synchronize their feeding with low tides when their preferred prey is exposed, and they've learned to time their activities precisely with tidal cycles, often roosting during high tide periods. They're devoted parents who lead their young on extensive foraging expeditions along the shore, teaching them essential skills for finding and opening shellfish, with family groups staying together for several months after hatching.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These ground-walking warblers are constantly in motion, bobbing their tails and rear ends almost continuously while foraging, a behavior so distinctive it makes them easy to identify even at a distance. They're aquatic specialists who wade through shallow water like tiny herons, picking insects and larvae from the surface and occasionally diving completely underwater in pursuit of prey. These long-distance migrants undertake remarkable journeys from their boreal breeding grounds to tropical wintering areas in Central and South America, with some individuals traveling over 5,000 miles each way. They're territorial singers whose loud, ringing songs can carry over half a mile through dense forest, and males often sing from prominent perches near water to advertise their territories to potential mates and rivals.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These rock-dwelling acrobats have flattened skulls and flexible bodies that allow them to squeeze into incredibly narrow rock crevices, sometimes disappearing completely into cracks barely wider than their bodies. They're musical cascaders whose songs are among the most beautiful in the bird world, consisting of a series of descending notes that echo hauntingly through canyon walls and can be heard over a mile away. These specialized climbers have extra-long toes and curved claws that allow them to walk up and down vertical rock faces with ease, and they can even hang upside down from cliff overhangs while foraging for spiders and insects. They're water-independent desert dwellers who obtain all their moisture from their prey and rarely need to drink, making them perfectly adapted to life in some of North America's most arid environments.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These split-personality warblers exist as two distinct populations that rarely interact: eastern birds that migrate through the Gulf of Mexico to Central America, and western birds that travel down the Pacific coast to Mexico, essentially functioning as separate species. They're ground nesters who build their well-hidden nests on the forest floor under dense vegetation, often at the base of trees or shrubs where they're nearly impossible to find without careful searching. These active foragers are constantly in motion, flicking their wings and tails while gleaning insects from leaves and bark, and they're particularly fond of hunting for caterpillars and aphids in the outer branches of trees. They're habitat specialists who prefer young forests and forest edges, thriving in areas that have been disturbed by logging, fire, or natural tree falls, making them beneficiaries of certain types of forest management.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These aggressive water birds are surprisingly violent fighters who engage in brutal territorial battles, using their sharp claws to rake opponents and sometimes fighting to the death over prime marsh territory. They're lobed-toe swimmers who aren't actually ducks despite their duck-like appearance, and their unique feet with lobed toes rather than webbed feet make them excellent swimmers while also allowing them to walk on floating vegetation. These devoted parents build multiple nests and often continue adding material throughout the breeding season, and their young are among the most colorful baby birds in North America with bright red and orange heads that fade to black as they mature. They're omnivorous opportunists who eat everything from aquatic plants and algae to fish, frogs, and even small birds, and they're known to steal food from other waterfowl and dive to depths of up to 25 feet when foraging.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These mysterious seabirds remained one of North America's greatest ornithological puzzles until 1974 when their first nest was finally discovered high in an old-growth tree, making them the last North American bird species to have their nesting habits documented. They're ancient forest commuters who nest on large moss-covered branches of old-growth conifers up to 150 feet above ground and up to 50 miles inland, then fly to the ocean daily to feed on small fish and marine invertebrates. These underwater fliers use their wings to 'fly' underwater while pursuing fish, and they're capable of diving to depths of over 100 feet, making them equally at home in air and water. They're conservation-dependent birds whose populations have declined dramatically due to old-growth forest loss, and they're considered an indicator species for the health of both marine and old-growth forest ecosystems.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tail-dipping flycatchers are the only Empidonax flycatcher that consistently pumps its tail downward rather than upward, a unique behavior that makes them identifiable even when silent among their notoriously difficult-to-identify relatives. They're sagebrush specialists who are closely tied to healthy sagebrush ecosystems and are considered an indicator species for sagebrush habitat quality, preferring areas with tall, dense sagebrush for nesting and foraging. These long-distance migrants travel from their western North American breeding grounds to wintering areas in Mexico, and they're one of the latest spring migrants among flycatchers, often not arriving on breeding grounds until late May or early June. They're patient hunters who often sit motionless for long periods on exposed perches before making quick sallying flights to catch flying insects, and they're particularly fond of hunting for flying ants and small beetles.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These desert specialists are perfectly adapted to life in some of North America's hottest and driest environments, and they can survive in areas where temperatures regularly exceed 110°F by entering torpor during the hottest parts of the day. They're early breeders who time their nesting to coincide with desert wildflower blooms, often starting to nest in February or March when most other birds are still on their wintering grounds. These aerial acrobats perform spectacular courtship displays where males climb high into the sky and then dive at tremendous speeds while producing loud whistling sounds with their tail feathers. They're nomadic wanderers who follow blooming cycles of desert plants, and their movements are so tied to flower availability that they can appear and disappear from areas seemingly overnight as nectar sources change.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These secretive grassland birds are named for their insect-like buzzing song that sounds remarkably similar to a grasshopper's call, and they're so secretive that they're more often heard than seen in their prairie habitats. They're ground nesters who build incredibly well-hidden nests in dense grass clumps, often with a partial dome or canopy of woven grass that makes them nearly impossible to find even when you know the general location. These habitat specialists require large expanses of native grassland and are considered an indicator species for healthy prairie ecosystems, declining dramatically as grasslands are converted to agriculture. They're unusual among sparrows for feeding their young almost exclusively insects during the breeding season, switching to a seed-based diet only after the young have fledged, and they're capable of running through dense grass with mouse-like agility.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These highly social birds live in complex flocks that can number in the hundreds and maintain sophisticated social hierarchies with dominant pairs leading the group and making decisions about when and where to move. They're seed-caching specialists who can remember the locations of thousands of buried pine nuts, and their remarkable spatial memory allows them to relocate cached seeds months later even under snow cover. These nomadic wanderers follow pinyon pine cone crops across the landscape, and their movements are so tied to cone production that they can disappear from an area for years when cone crops fail. They're cooperative breeders where non-breeding individuals help feed and protect the young of breeding pairs, and their complex social structure includes sentries who watch for predators while the flock feeds.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These large forest pigeons are North America's only native pigeon and are closely related to the extinct Passenger Pigeon, sharing similar flocking behaviors and forest habitat preferences. They're nomadic fruit-followers who travel great distances to find ripening berries and acorns, and their movements are so unpredictable that they can be abundant in an area one year and completely absent the next. These mineral-seeking birds regularly visit natural salt licks and mineral springs, and they're often seen at clay banks and mineral deposits where they ingest essential minerals needed for their health and reproduction. They're powerful fliers capable of reaching speeds over 50 mph, and their strong flight muscles allow them to travel hundreds of miles in search of food sources, making them one of the most mobile birds in western North America.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These plain gray birds are habitat specialists who are almost entirely restricted to oak woodlands and are considered an indicator species for healthy oak ecosystem conditions throughout California and Oregon. They're year-round residents who form lifelong pair bonds and maintain territories in the same oak groves for their entire lives, with some pairs using the same nest cavity for multiple years. These acrobatic foragers are constantly in motion, hanging upside down from oak branches and twigs while searching for insects, and they're particularly skilled at finding hidden caterpillars and aphids among oak leaves. They're cavity nesters who excavate their own nest holes in soft, decaying oak wood, and they often line their nests with animal fur, feathers, and soft plant materials to create a cozy environment for their young.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These marathon migrants undertake one of the most incredible journeys in the bird world, flying non-stop over the Atlantic Ocean from eastern North America to South America, a journey of up to 2,300 miles that can take 72-88 hours of continuous flight. They're weight-gain specialists who can nearly double their body weight before migration, accumulating fat reserves that comprise up to 50% of their total body weight to fuel their epic ocean crossing. These late migrants are among the last warblers to arrive on breeding grounds in spring and the first to leave in fall, with some individuals beginning their southward journey as early as July. They're insectivorous specialists during breeding season but switch to a fruit-based diet during migration, gorging on berries to build up the fat reserves necessary for their transoceanic flight.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These predatory songbirds are known as 'butcher birds' for their habit of impaling prey on thorns and barbed wire, creating gruesome larders of mice, small birds, and large insects that they can return to later when hunting is poor. They're irruptive visitors from the Arctic who appear in northern states during winter when prey becomes scarce in their breeding grounds, and their numbers can vary dramatically from year to year. These patient hunters often sit motionless on prominent perches for long periods, scanning for prey with their keen eyesight before making swift attacks that can include chasing down small birds in flight. They're surprisingly powerful for songbirds, capable of killing prey as large as small mammals and other birds, using their hooked bills to deliver fatal bites to the neck or head of their victims.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These elegant shorebirds are distinguished from their larger Greater Yellowlegs cousins by their more delicate build, straighter bills, and different feeding behavior, often picking at the water surface rather than probing deeply into mud. They're long-distance migrants who breed in the boreal forests of Canada and Alaska, often nesting near small ponds and bogs in areas so remote that their breeding biology was poorly known until recent decades. These social birds often feed in mixed flocks with other shorebird species, and they're known for their nervous, alert behavior, often being the first to sound alarm calls when predators approach. They're versatile foragers who wade in shallow water picking up small fish, aquatic insects, and crustaceans, and they're capable of swimming when necessary, unlike many other shorebird species.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny shorebirds are the world's smallest sandpipers, weighing less than an ounce yet capable of incredible migrations that can take them from Arctic breeding grounds to South American wintering areas. They're yellow-legged specialists among the 'peeps' (small sandpipers), and their yellowish legs help distinguish them from other similar species that have black legs. These nervous feeders are constantly in motion, running along shorelines and mudflats with rapid, mouse-like movements while picking up tiny invertebrates, and they often feed in areas with softer substrates than other sandpipers. They're flexible habitat users who can be found not only on coastal mudflats but also at inland ponds, sewage treatment plants, and even flooded agricultural fields during migration.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These secretive marsh birds have laterally compressed bodies that allow them to slip through dense cattail and sedge stands like feathered mice, giving rise to the phrase 'thin as a rail.' They're vocal communicators who are more often heard than seen, producing a variety of calls including their distinctive 'kid-dick' call that sounds like someone tapping on wood. These versatile swimmers can dive underwater when threatened and are capable of swimming considerable distances, and they can even walk on floating vegetation using their long, unwebbed toes. They're opportunistic omnivores who eat everything from aquatic invertebrates and small fish to seeds and berries, and they're known to hunt at night as well as during the day, using their long bills to probe in mud and shallow water.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These forest drummers are famous for their thunderous drumming displays where males beat their wings rapidly while standing on fallen logs, creating a sound that starts slowly and accelerates into a blur, audible up to a quarter mile away. They're explosive fliers who can burst from cover with startling speed and noise, often causing heart-stopping moments for hikers who accidentally flush them from dense undergrowth. These snow-adapted birds grow feather 'snowshoes' on their feet during winter that act like natural snowshoes, allowing them to walk on top of snow and roost in snow burrows for insulation. They're cyclic populations whose numbers rise and fall in roughly 10-year cycles tied to predator-prey relationships, and during peak years they can be remarkably abundant before crashing to very low numbers.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These 'camp robbers' are incredibly tame and curious birds who will boldly approach campers and hikers to investigate food opportunities, often landing on people's heads or shoulders while looking for handouts. They're food-hoarding specialists who cache thousands of food items throughout their territories, using their sticky saliva to glue food to tree bark and branches where it can be retrieved months later. These cold-adapted birds are among the few species that breed in the depths of winter, starting to nest in February or March when temperatures can be well below freezing, and they time their breeding to coincide with peak food availability. They're family-oriented birds where young from previous years often help their parents raise new broods, and they maintain complex social hierarchies within their family groups.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These secretive sparrows are among the most difficult North American sparrows to observe, preferring to skulk in dense vegetation and rarely venturing into the open, making them a prized sighting for birders. They're habitat specialists who prefer wet meadows, bogs, and willow thickets, and they're considered an indicator species for healthy wetland edge habitats. These nervous birds are constantly alert and will freeze motionless when threatened, relying on their streaked plumage to blend perfectly with dried grasses and sedges. They're long-distance migrants who breed across the boreal forest and western mountains but winter primarily in Mexico, undertaking journeys of thousands of miles between their breeding and wintering grounds.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These aquatic songbirds are the only North American bird that can walk underwater, using their wings to 'fly' beneath the surface while hunting for aquatic insects and small fish in fast-flowing mountain streams. They're constantly bobbing and dipping their bodies up and down, a behavior that gives them their name and may help them see through the surface glare of moving water. These cold-water specialists have special adaptations including extra-dense feathers, enlarged oil glands for waterproofing, and flaps that can close their nostrils underwater, allowing them to forage in near-freezing water. They're year-round residents along mountain streams and will continue feeding underwater even when streams are partially frozen, and they build their dome-shaped nests behind waterfalls or on cliff faces near rushing water.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These secretive marsh birds are more often heard than seen, producing a distinctive descending whinny call that sounds like a horse's neigh echoing through cattail marshes. They're compressed-body specialists whose laterally flattened bodies allow them to slip through dense marsh vegetation with ease, and they can virtually disappear into vegetation that seems too sparse to hide a bird. These versatile swimmers can dive underwater when threatened and are capable of swimming considerable distances, and they can even walk on floating vegetation using their long, unwebbed toes. They're opportunistic omnivores who eat everything from aquatic invertebrates and small fish to seeds and marsh plants, and they're known to climb up cattail stalks to reach seeds, showing remarkable agility for a rail.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These fish-eating ducks have serrated bills with tooth-like projections that help them grip slippery fish, and they're capable of catching fish up to half their own body length. They're diving specialists who can stay underwater for up to a minute while pursuing fish, using their powerful webbed feet for propulsion and their streamlined bodies to chase prey through the water. These cavity nesters often use nest boxes or natural tree cavities up to 100 feet above ground, and their ducklings must make a dramatic leap from the nest cavity to the ground or water below when they're ready to leave. They're social birds during winter, forming large rafts on open water that can number in the hundreds or thousands, and they often feed cooperatively by herding fish into shallow areas.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These part-bird, part-submarine aquatic acrobats have feet positioned near their rear ends (their Latin name 'podylimbus' literally means 'feet at the buttocks'), making them superb underwater propulsion systems but hilariously awkward on land. They're living submarines with the remarkable ability to trap water in their feathers, giving them precise control over their buoyancy so they can sink deeply, hover just below the surface, or expose exactly as much of their body as they wish. These feather-eating specialists consume large quantities of their own plumage—sometimes filling more than half their stomach—which forms a sieve-like plug that prevents hard prey parts from entering their intestines and helps form indigestible pellets they can regurgitate. They're dramatic escape artists who perform spectacular 'crash-dives' when threatened, pushing their bodies down with wings thrust outward while kicking water several feet into the air as their tail and head disappear last, and despite being poor fliers, rare individuals have somehow managed to reach the Hawaiian Islands, Europe, and even the Canary Islands.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These filter-feeding ducks have enormous spatulate bills equipped with comb-like projections called lamellae that allow them to strain tiny organisms from water like living sieves. They're spinning feeders who often swim in tight circles while feeding, creating small whirlpools that bring food particles to the surface where they can be more easily captured. These social foragers often feed in groups, with multiple birds swimming in formation to stir up food and take advantage of each other's feeding activities. They're early migrants who are among the first ducks to head south in fall and among the last to return north in spring, and they're capable of long-distance flights between breeding and wintering areas.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These colonial nesters excavate tunnels up to 5 feet deep in sandy banks and cliffs, with hundreds or thousands of pairs creating honeycomb-like colonies that can be visible from great distances. They're the smallest North American swallow and are found on every continent except Antarctica and Australia, making them one of the most widely distributed birds in the world. These aerial insectivores catch all their food on the wing and are capable of incredible aerial maneuvers, often feeding just inches above water surfaces or through dense swarms of flying insects. They're declining rapidly across much of their range due to habitat loss and pesticide use, and they're considered a species of conservation concern in many areas.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These striking marsh birds are highly polygamous, with dominant males maintaining territories that can include up to 15 females, while subordinate males may not breed at all. They're aggressive territory defenders who will attack much larger birds including hawks and herons that venture too close to their nesting colonies in cattail marshes. These social nesters form dense colonies where hundreds of pairs may nest in close proximity, creating a cacophony of harsh calls and aggressive interactions throughout the breeding season. They're nomadic wanderers outside the breeding season, forming massive flocks that can number in the tens of thousands as they move across agricultural areas in search of grain and insects.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These ethereal singers produce one of the most beautiful songs in North American forests, a downward-spiraling flute-like melody that seems to echo and reverberate through the woods even when sung by a single bird. They're ground foragers who spend most of their time scratching through leaf litter like tiny chickens, using both feet to kick aside leaves while searching for insects and other invertebrates. These long-distance migrants travel from their North American breeding grounds to spend winter in the Amazon basin, undertaking journeys of over 5,000 miles each way. They're declining rapidly across much of their range due to habitat fragmentation and are considered an indicator species for healthy mature forest ecosystems.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These aerial specialists are completely dependent on human-provided housing in eastern North America, with virtually all eastern populations nesting in martin houses, gourds, or other artificial structures provided by dedicated martin landlords. They're the largest North American swallow and are capable of incredible aerial feats, catching all their food on the wing and even drinking by skimming water surfaces while flying. These social birds form large communal roosts during migration that can include tens of thousands of individuals, creating spectacular aerial displays as they gather at traditional roosting sites. They're long-distance migrants who travel to South America for winter, and their populations have declined significantly due to competition from introduced species like European Starlings and House Sparrows for nesting cavities.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These large shorebirds undertake some of the longest migrations in the bird world, with some individuals flying non-stop for over 4,000 miles from Alaska to South America, using fat reserves that can comprise up to 55% of their body weight. They're specialized foragers with long, curved bills perfectly adapted for extracting crabs, worms, and other invertebrates from deep burrows in mudflats and sandy beaches. These vocal birds have distinctive calls that can be heard over a mile away, and they often call while flying, helping to keep flocks together during long migrations. They're declining rapidly across much of their range due to habitat loss on both breeding and wintering grounds, and they're considered a species of high conservation concern.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These aggressive territorial defenders are among the most pugnacious of all hummingbirds, fearlessly attacking birds many times their size including hawks, crows, and even humans who venture too close to their territories. They're early migrants who arrive on their California breeding grounds as early as January, often before many flowers have bloomed, and they time their breeding to coincide with peak wildflower seasons. These aerial acrobats perform spectacular courtship displays involving dramatic dives from heights of up to 100 feet, creating loud buzzing sounds with their tail feathers during high-speed dives. They're habitat specialists closely tied to coastal scrub and chaparral environments, and they're considered an indicator species for healthy California coastal ecosystems.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These powerful coastal predators are among the most aggressive gulls in North America, capable of killing and eating other seabirds including smaller gulls, terns, and even young pelicans. They're intelligent tool users who have learned to drop shellfish from great heights onto rocks to crack them open, and they can recognize individual humans who pose threats to their colonies. These long-lived birds can survive for over 25 years and often return to the same nesting colonies year after year, with some individuals using the same nest site for multiple seasons. They're opportunistic scavengers who have adapted well to human presence, often following fishing boats and scavenging at garbage dumps, but they're also skilled hunters capable of catching fish, squid, and marine invertebrates.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These 'prairie gulls' are unusual among gulls for breeding primarily in inland freshwater marshes rather than coastal areas, and they're highly nomadic, following insect outbreaks and agricultural activities across the Great Plains. They're beneficial agricultural birds who consume vast quantities of harmful insects, and they're famous for following farm equipment to catch insects stirred up by plowing and harvesting activities. These social birds form dense breeding colonies that can include thousands of pairs, and they're known for their synchronized breeding cycles where entire colonies will lay eggs within a few days of each other. They're long-distance migrants who travel from their prairie breeding grounds to wintering areas along the Pacific coast of South America, undertaking journeys of over 5,000 miles each way.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These high-altitude specialists are among the highest-breeding birds in North America, nesting at elevations up to 14,000 feet in alpine environments where few other birds can survive. They're cold-adapted birds with special throat pouches that allow them to carry large quantities of seeds back to their young, and they can survive in temperatures well below freezing. These nomadic wanderers follow snow lines and weather patterns, moving to lower elevations during severe weather and returning to high peaks when conditions improve. They're social birds that form large flocks during winter, often mixing with other rosy-finch species, and they're known for their fearless behavior around humans at ski areas and mountain research stations.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These intelligent corvids are accomplished mimics who can imitate the calls of hawks so accurately that they can clear bird feeders of other species, allowing them to feed without competition. They're acorn-planting foresters who cache thousands of acorns each fall, and their remarkable spatial memory allows them to relocate buried nuts months later, making them essential for oak forest regeneration. These social birds have complex communication systems with over 20 different vocalizations, and they can recognize individual humans and remember those who pose threats to their nests. They're partial migrants where some populations migrate south while others remain year-round, and their migration patterns can vary dramatically from year to year based on food availability.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These distinctive sparrows have bold facial patterns that make them one of the most easily identified sparrows in North America, with their striking black, white, and chestnut head markings visible from considerable distances. They're ground nesters who build their nests in slight depressions on the ground, often under the protection of a small shrub or grass clump, and they're known for their elaborate courtship displays involving wing-spreading and tail-fanning. These social birds often gather in large flocks during migration and winter, and they're known for their beautiful, melodious songs that include liquid notes and trills. They're declining across much of their range due to habitat loss and are considered a species of conservation concern in many areas.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These 'butcher birds' are predatory songbirds who impale their prey on thorns, barbed wire, and sharp twigs, creating gruesome larders of insects, small mammals, and birds that they can return to when hunting is poor. They're declining rapidly across North America and are considered one of the fastest-declining songbirds on the continent, with populations dropping by over 75% since the 1960s. These patient hunters often sit motionless on prominent perches for long periods, scanning for prey with their keen eyesight before making swift attacks on insects, small rodents, and even other birds. They're surprisingly powerful for their size, capable of killing prey as large as small birds and mammals, using their hooked bills to deliver fatal bites to the neck or head.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These sap-drilling woodpeckers create neat rows of holes in tree bark to access the sweet sap beneath, and their wells also attract insects that get stuck in the sap, providing a protein-rich supplement to their diet. They're keystone species whose sap wells are used by over 35 other bird species, numerous mammals, and countless insects, making them ecosystem engineers that benefit entire forest communities. These methodical workers maintain their sap wells throughout the breeding season, returning regularly to drill new holes and maintain existing ones, and they show strong site fidelity to productive sap trees. They're partially migratory birds where some populations move to lower elevations in winter while others remain year-round, and they're closely tied to healthy coniferous and mixed forests of the Pacific Northwest.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These hardy northern birds are the only chickadees with brown caps and are perfectly adapted to survive brutal winters in the boreal forest, where they can endure temperatures as low as -40°F by entering controlled hypothermia at night. They're food-hoarding specialists who cache thousands of food items throughout their territories, using their excellent spatial memory to relocate hidden seeds and insects months later when food is scarce. These acrobatic foragers are constantly in motion, hanging upside down from conifer branches while searching for insects and seeds, and they're particularly fond of the seeds from spruce and fir cones. They're irruptive wanderers whose movements south depend on cone crop failures in the boreal forest, and during invasion years they can appear at bird feeders far from their normal range, delighting birders with their tame and curious behavior.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These introduced European gamebirds form tight family groups called coveys that huddle together in circular formations during cold weather, with all birds facing outward to watch for predators while conserving body heat. They're explosive fliers who burst from cover with startling speed and whirring wings when flushed, often scattering in different directions before regrouping later through soft contact calls. These ground-dwelling birds are perfectly camouflaged for life in agricultural areas, and they're so well-adapted to farmland that they're considered beneficial to farmers for consuming large quantities of weed seeds and harmful insects. They're declining across much of their North American range due to changes in farming practices, particularly the increased use of pesticides and the loss of hedgerows and field margins that provide essential cover.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These fire-following specialists are among the first birds to colonize recently burned forests, where they feast on wood-boring beetle larvae that thrive in fire-killed trees, and they can detect the movement of insects under bark from remarkable distances. They're powerful excavators with incredibly strong neck muscles and reinforced skulls that allow them to chisel through the hardest wood, and they're the only North American woodpecker with a solid black back. These nomadic wanderers follow insect outbreaks and forest disturbances across the landscape, and their presence is often an indicator of healthy forest fire cycles and natural disturbance patterns. They're cavity nesters who excavate their own nest holes in dead or dying trees, and their abandoned cavities provide essential nesting sites for many other forest species including flying squirrels, martens, and smaller birds.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny seabirds spend virtually their entire lives at sea, coming to land only to breed on remote islands, and they're so adapted to oceanic life that they can drink seawater and excrete excess salt through special glands near their nostrils. They're nocturnal on land to avoid predation by gulls and other seabirds, and they navigate to their burrows in complete darkness using their excellent sense of smell to locate their specific nest site among thousands of others. These storm riders are perfectly adapted to life in rough seas, using their tube-shaped nostrils to breathe while skimming just inches above wave crests, and they can ride out severe storms that would be deadly to larger seabirds. They're long-lived birds that can survive for over 30 years, and they show remarkable site fidelity, often returning to the same burrow year after year and maintaining long-term pair bonds with the same mate.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These California specialists are found almost exclusively in oak woodlands and are considered an indicator species for healthy oak ecosystem conditions, preferring areas with a mix of live oaks, valley oaks, and riparian woodlands. They're acorn specialists who have co-evolved with California's oak trees, and they're particularly skilled at extracting acorn weevil larvae from infested acorns, making them beneficial to oak forest health. These agile climbers are constantly in motion, spiraling up and around tree trunks and branches while searching for insects, and they're known for their distinctive rattling call that echoes through oak groves. They're year-round residents who maintain territories in the same oak woodlands throughout their lives, and they often excavate multiple roosting cavities that they use for shelter during cold weather and storms.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These mysterious birds are North America's largest wood-warbler but are so unusual that scientists debate whether they actually belong in the warbler family, with recent genetic studies suggesting they may be in a family of their own. They're secretive skulkers who prefer dense thickets and shrublands, and despite their large size and loud vocalizations, they can be incredibly difficult to observe as they move through tangled vegetation like feathered ghosts. These vocal virtuosos produce an amazing variety of sounds including whistles, chucks, rattles, and even mechanical-sounding notes, and they often sing from hidden perches or during spectacular flight displays where they dangle their legs and flutter slowly above the vegetation. They're declining rapidly across much of their range due to habitat loss, particularly the conversion of shrubland and early successional habitats to development and agriculture.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These diving ducks are misnamed because their 'ring' is actually around their bill, not their neck, though males do have a faint chestnut collar that's usually invisible in the field, making 'Ring-billed Duck' a more accurate name. They're versatile divers who can feed both by diving underwater and by dabbling at the surface, and they're capable of diving to depths of up to 40 feet while foraging for aquatic plants, seeds, and invertebrates. These social birds often form large rafts during migration and winter, sometimes mixing with other diving duck species, and they're known for their distinctive peaked head shape that helps distinguish them from similar species. They're adaptable nesters who prefer small ponds and marshes with emergent vegetation for breeding, and they're one of the few diving ducks that regularly nest in temporary wetlands that may dry up during the breeding season.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These small owls come in two distinct color morphs—red and gray—that persist in the same populations, with the color determined by genetics rather than age, sex, or season, and both morphs can occur in the same brood. They're remarkably adaptable birds who have learned to thrive in suburban and urban environments, often nesting in nest boxes, tree cavities, and even unusual locations like mailboxes and decorative planters. These versatile predators have an incredibly diverse diet that includes everything from insects and earthworms to small mammals, birds, fish, and even crayfish, making them one of the most opportunistic owls in North America. They're vocal communicators with a variety of calls including their distinctive descending whinny and monotonic trill, and they're known for their fearless defense of their nest sites, sometimes attacking much larger intruders including humans.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These California endemics are found nowhere else in the world except the Central Valley and adjacent foothills of California, making them one of the most geographically restricted birds in North America. They're highly social birds who live in complex family groups and maintain intricate social hierarchies, with young birds often helping their parents raise subsequent broods in a cooperative breeding system. These intelligent corvids are accomplished tool users and problem solvers, and they're known for their elaborate funeral behavior where groups will gather around deceased magpies and call loudly for extended periods. They're declining rapidly due to habitat loss, West Nile virus, and other threats, and they're considered a species of conservation concern with populations dropping by over 60% since the 1960s.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These sea ducks are perfectly adapted to life in rough coastal waters, using their powerful webbed feet and streamlined bodies to dive through crashing surf while foraging for mussels, clams, and other shellfish. They're long-distance migrants who breed in remote areas of the boreal forest and tundra, often nesting near small ponds and lakes hundreds of miles from the ocean where they'll eventually spend their winters. These social birds form large rafts during winter that can number in the thousands, creating spectacular concentrations along rocky coastlines where they feed in the surf zone. They're sexually dimorphic with males sporting distinctive white patches on their heads and colorful bills, while females are more subdued brown birds, and both sexes have the characteristic sloping profile that gives them their unique silhouette.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These small dark geese are eelgrass specialists who time their migrations to coincide with the growth cycles of their preferred food, and they're so dependent on eelgrass that population crashes in the 1930s nearly drove them to extinction when disease wiped out eelgrass beds. They're Arctic breeders who nest on the tundra in some of the most remote and harsh environments on Earth, and their young must be ready to migrate within just a few months of hatching to escape the approaching Arctic winter. These social birds form large flocks during migration and winter, and they're known for their distinctive rolling flight pattern and their habit of feeding in shallow water by tipping forward like dabbling ducks. They're long-lived birds that can survive for over 20 years, and they show strong site fidelity to both breeding and wintering areas, often returning to the same locations year after year.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These large shorebirds are among the most widespread birds in the world, breeding in the high Arctic and wintering on coastlines of every continent except Antarctica, making them true global citizens. They're visual hunters who use a distinctive stop-and-go foraging technique, running quickly across mudflats and beaches before stopping abruptly to scan for prey, then striking with lightning-fast precision. These dramatic seasonal transformers undergo one of the most striking plumage changes of any shorebird, molting from their bold black-and-white breeding plumage to subtle gray winter colors that provide perfect camouflage on sandy beaches. They're sentinel species whose loud alarm calls alert other shorebirds to approaching danger, and they're often the first to take flight when predators appear, leading entire mixed flocks to safety.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These soaring scavengers have an extraordinary sense of smell that allows them to detect carrion from miles away, making them one of the few birds that relies primarily on scent rather than sight to find food. They're thermal masters who can soar for hours without flapping their wings, using rising columns of warm air to gain altitude and cover vast distances while searching for food with minimal energy expenditure. These ecosystem cleaners play a crucial role in preventing the spread of disease by consuming carrion that would otherwise rot and harbor dangerous bacteria, and their powerful stomach acid can neutralize toxins that would be deadly to other animals. They're surprisingly social birds who often roost communally in large groups, and they're known for their distinctive defensive behavior of vomiting on threats, which is both effective and memorable for potential predators.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These sea ducks are the most marine of all North American ducks, spending virtually their entire lives in saltwater environments and rarely venturing into freshwater except during breeding season. They're powerful divers who can descend to depths of over 60 feet while foraging for mollusks, crustaceans, and marine worms, using their strong bills to pry shellfish from rocks and sandy bottoms. These social birds form large flocks during winter that can stretch for miles along coastlines, creating some of the most impressive waterfowl concentrations in North America. They're long-distance migrants who breed in remote areas of Alaska and northern Canada, often nesting near small tundra ponds, and they undertake epic journeys to reach their coastal wintering areas along both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These intelligent corvids were recently split from the Western Scrub-Jay complex and are named after Samuel Washington Woodhouse, a 19th-century naturalist who explored the American Southwest. They're acorn-caching specialists who bury thousands of acorns each fall and can remember the locations of their caches for months, playing a crucial role in oak forest regeneration across their range. These social birds live in complex family groups where young birds often remain with their parents for extended periods, helping to defend territory and sometimes assisting with raising subsequent broods. They're fearless nest defenders who will aggressively mob much larger predators including hawks, owls, and even humans who venture too close to their nesting areas, using coordinated attacks and loud alarm calls to drive away threats.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These forest hawks are famous for their spectacular migration spectacle called 'kettles,' where thousands of individuals spiral upward together in thermal columns, creating some of the most impressive raptor concentrations in North America. They're secretive forest nesters who prefer mature deciduous and mixed forests, and despite being relatively common, they're often overlooked due to their quiet nature and preference for staying hidden in the forest canopy. These patient hunters often sit motionless for long periods on concealed perches, waiting for small mammals, amphibians, and insects to move within striking distance before making swift, precise attacks. They're long-distance migrants who travel from their North American breeding grounds to wintering areas in Central and South America, with some individuals flying over 4,000 miles each way.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These tiny dynamos are constantly in motion, flicking their tails and wings while gleaning insects from leaves and bark, and they're so active that they can appear almost hummingbird-like as they hover and dart through the foliage. They're master architects who build some of the most beautiful nests in North America, creating deep cups covered with lichens and spider webs that look like natural knots on tree branches. These vocal birds have surprisingly loud voices for their size, producing a variety of calls and songs, and males are particularly vocal during breeding season when they sing almost continuously while foraging. They're expanding their range northward, possibly in response to climate change, and they're now breeding in areas where they were historically absent, making them an interesting species for studying range shifts.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These small shorebirds are named for the partial webbing between their toes that helps them walk on soft sand and mud, and they're perfectly designed for life on beaches and mudflats with their compact bodies and short, straight bills. They're visual hunters who use the classic plover feeding technique of running quickly across the sand, stopping abruptly to scan for prey, then striking with lightning-fast precision to capture small invertebrates. These Arctic breeders nest on the tundra in simple scrapes lined with pebbles and vegetation, and their young are precocial, able to run and feed themselves within hours of hatching. They're long-distance migrants who travel from their Arctic breeding grounds to wintering areas throughout the Americas, with some individuals flying non-stop for over 1,800 miles during migration.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These declining blackbirds have experienced one of the most dramatic population crashes of any North American songbird, with numbers dropping by over 85% since the 1960s, making them a species of urgent conservation concern. They're wetland specialists who prefer swampy areas, beaver ponds, and boggy forests, and they're considered an indicator species for healthy boreal wetland ecosystems. These seasonal transformers get their name from the rusty edges on their feathers during fall and winter, which wear off by spring to reveal glossy black plumage in males and dark gray in females. They're opportunistic foragers who wade through shallow water like tiny herons, picking up aquatic insects, small fish, and invertebrates, and they're one of the few blackbirds that regularly feeds in water.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These desert-adapted flycatchers are remarkably tolerant of hot, dry conditions and can survive in areas where summer temperatures regularly exceed 110°F, obtaining most of their water from their insect prey. They're cavity nesters who often use unusual nest sites including mailboxes, fence posts, and even old shoes or cans, and they're known for incorporating snake skins into their nest construction, possibly as a deterrent to predators. These patient hunters often sit motionless on exposed perches for long periods before making quick sallying flights to catch flying insects, and they're particularly fond of hunting for bees, wasps, and flying beetles. They're partial migrants where some populations move south for winter while others remain year-round, and their movements are often tied to local weather patterns and food availability.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These remarkable colonizers naturally expanded their range from Africa to South America in the 1930s, then spread throughout the Americas in one of the most dramatic range expansions in recorded bird history, reaching North America by the 1950s. They're commensal feeders who have formed a mutually beneficial relationship with large grazing mammals, following cattle, horses, and other livestock to catch insects stirred up by their movement. These adaptable birds have learned to exploit human-modified landscapes, and they're often seen following farm equipment, lawn mowers, and even golf course maintenance vehicles to catch disturbed insects. They're social nesters who form large colonies often mixed with other heron species, and during breeding season they develop beautiful orange-buff plumes on their heads, backs, and breasts.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These active warblers are constantly in motion, fanning their tails and drooping their wings to flash their bright orange and black patches, a behavior that may startle insects into flight where they can be more easily caught. They're delayed-plumage birds where young males don't acquire their full adult plumage until their second year, and first-year males in female-like plumage are often called 'she-males' by birders. These versatile foragers use multiple feeding techniques including gleaning insects from leaves, catching flies in midair, and even hovering briefly to pick insects from the undersides of leaves. They're long-distance migrants who travel from their North American breeding grounds to wintering areas in Central America and the Caribbean, and they're considered an indicator species for healthy mature forest ecosystems.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These sewing-machine shorebirds are named for their rapid probing technique, where they insert their long bills deep into mud and probe with rapid up-and-down motions that resemble a sewing machine needle. They're freshwater specialists who prefer inland wetlands, flooded fields, and shallow ponds, and they can be distinguished from their Short-billed Dowitcher cousins by their preference for freshwater habitats and their distinctive calls. These social birds often feed in tight flocks, creating a synchronized feeding spectacle as dozens of birds probe the mud in unison, and they're known for their tameness, often allowing close approach by birders. They're long-distance migrants who breed in Alaska and western Canada and winter from the southern United States to Central America, with some individuals traveling over 5,000 miles each way.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These Arctic breeders are the smallest and most widespread of all loons, and they're the only loon species that can take off from land, allowing them to nest on small ponds that would be too small for other loon species. They're fish-eating specialists with dagger-like bills and streamlined bodies perfectly adapted for underwater pursuit, and they can dive to depths of over 200 feet while chasing fish. These vocal birds produce haunting calls that carry for miles across the tundra, and their wailing cries are considered one of the most evocative sounds of the Arctic wilderness. They're long-distance migrants who travel from their Arctic breeding grounds to coastal wintering areas, and they're capable of flying at speeds over 60 mph during migration.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These elegant loons are perfectly adapted to life in both freshwater and marine environments, breeding on tundra lakes and wintering along Pacific coastlines from Alaska to Baja California. They're powerful swimmers who use their feet for propulsion underwater and can stay submerged for over a minute while pursuing fish, and their solid bones help them achieve neutral buoyancy for efficient diving. These social birds often gather in large flocks during migration and winter, sometimes forming rafts of hundreds or thousands of individuals in coastal waters. They're vocal communicators whose haunting calls include wails, tremolos, and yodels that can carry for miles, and their calls are an iconic sound of northern wilderness areas.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These sap-drilling woodpeckers create neat rows of holes in tree bark to access sweet sap, and their wells become feeding stations for over 35 other bird species, numerous mammals, and countless insects, making them keystone species in their forest ecosystems. They're methodical workers who maintain their sap wells throughout the breeding season, returning regularly to drill new holes and tend existing ones, and they show strong site fidelity to productive sap trees. These partially migratory birds move to lower elevations during winter, and some populations migrate considerable distances to reach areas with suitable sap trees and milder weather. They're hybrid zone participants who interbreed with Red-breasted and Yellow-bellied Sapsuckers where their ranges overlap, creating complex identification challenges for birders in contact zones.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These small herons are among the few birds that regularly use tools, dropping insects, worms, or small objects onto the water surface to attract fish, demonstrating remarkable intelligence and problem-solving ability. They're patient hunters who can remain motionless for extended periods while waiting for prey to come within striking distance, then strike with lightning-fast precision using their sharp, dagger-like bills. These secretive birds prefer dense vegetation along water edges and are masters of camouflage, often freezing with their bills pointed upward to blend in with surrounding reeds and branches. They're surprisingly vocal for herons, producing a variety of calls including their distinctive 'kyow' call that echoes across wetlands, and they're known for their dramatic threat displays when defending territory.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These powerful forest raptors are the largest of the accipiters and are capable of taking prey as large as grouse, rabbits, and even small deer, making them apex predators in many forest ecosystems. They're incredibly agile fliers who can navigate through dense forest at high speeds, using their long tails as rudders and their broad wings for quick maneuvering between trees while pursuing prey. These fierce defenders are known for their aggressive protection of nesting areas, and they will fearlessly attack much larger intruders including humans, bears, and other raptors that venture too close to their nests. They're cyclic populations whose numbers fluctuate dramatically based on prey availability, particularly snowshoe hare and grouse populations, and during low prey years they may irrupt southward in search of food.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These plain brown birds are California endemics found almost exclusively within the state's borders, and they're so closely tied to California's chaparral and oak woodland habitats that they're considered an indicator species for these ecosystems. They're year-round residents who form lifelong pair bonds and maintain territories in the same areas throughout their lives, with some pairs using the same nesting sites for multiple years. These ground foragers spend most of their time scratching through leaf litter with both feet in a distinctive backward-hopping motion, searching for seeds, insects, and berries beneath shrubs and trees. They're surprisingly vocal birds with a variety of calls including their distinctive metallic 'chink' note, and they're known for their curious and relatively tame behavior around humans, often allowing close approach in parks and gardens.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These elegant waterbirds are master divers who can stay underwater for over a minute while pursuing fish, and they're capable of adjusting their buoyancy by trapping air in their feathers to control how deeply they float in the water. They're elaborate courtship performers who engage in synchronized swimming displays with their mates, including the famous 'weed ceremony' where pairs present each other with aquatic vegetation while swimming side by side. These seasonal transformers undergo dramatic plumage changes between breeding and winter, molting from their striking red necks and ornate head plumes to subdued gray and white winter colors. They're partially flightless during molt when they lose all their flight feathers at once, making them temporarily vulnerable but allowing them to regrow a complete new set of feathers for migration.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These Arctic breeders are the only North American hawks with feathered legs all the way to their toes, an adaptation that helps them survive in some of the coldest environments where any bird of prey breeds. They're irruptive migrants whose winter movements south depend on prey cycles in their Arctic breeding grounds, and during invasion years they can appear in large numbers across the northern United States. These patient hunters often hover in place while scanning for prey, a behavior that's unusual among buteos, and they're capable of hunting in weather conditions that would ground other raptors. They're dimorphic birds that come in both light and dark color morphs, with the proportion of each morph varying geographically and possibly related to different hunting strategies and prey preferences.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These secretive flycatchers are virtually impossible to distinguish from Willow Flycatchers by sight alone, and they were considered the same species until 1973 when scientists discovered they have completely different songs and habitat preferences. They're wetland specialists who prefer alder swamps, beaver ponds, and boggy areas, and they're considered an indicator species for healthy riparian and wetland edge habitats. These late migrants are among the last flycatchers to arrive on breeding grounds in spring, often not appearing until late May or early June, and they're also among the first to depart in fall. They're long-distance migrants who travel from their North American breeding grounds to wintering areas in South America, undertaking journeys of over 5,000 miles each way despite weighing less than half an ounce.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These sap-drilling woodpeckers are ecosystem engineers whose neat rows of sap wells provide food for over 35 other bird species, numerous mammals, and countless insects, making them keystone species in their forest communities. They're methodical workers who maintain their sap wells throughout the breeding season, returning regularly to drill new holes and tend existing ones, and they show remarkable site fidelity to productive sap trees. These migratory woodpeckers are unusual among their family for traveling long distances, with some individuals flying from Canada to Central America, and they're the only woodpecker species that's completely migratory throughout its range. They're sexually dimorphic with males sporting red throats and females having white throats, and both sexes develop the distinctive yellow wash on their bellies that gives them their name.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These mountain specialists are the smallest towhees and are perfectly adapted to life in high-elevation shrublands, preferring dense brush and chaparral between 5,000 and 11,000 feet elevation. They're secretive ground foragers who spend most of their time scratching through leaf litter beneath dense shrubs, using the distinctive towhee double-scratch technique of jumping forward and then quickly scratching backward with both feet.
