These accomplished singers produce some of the most complex and beautiful songs among sparrows, with males singing from prominent perches to advertise their territories and attract mates. They're altitudinal migrants who move to lower elevations during winter, and some populations migrate considerable distances to reach suitable wintering habitat in desert areas of the southwestern United States and Mexico.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These remarkable nightjars are the only birds known to enter true hibernation, with some individuals spending weeks or months in a state of torpor with dramatically reduced body temperature and metabolic rate during cold weather. They're perfectly camouflaged for their rocky desert habitats, and when roosting during the day they're virtually invisible against the ground, relying on their cryptic plumage to avoid detection by predators. These aerial insectivores have enormous mouths relative to their body size, and they hunt by flying low over the ground with their mouths open, scooping up moths, beetles, and other flying insects. They're vocal nighttime singers whose repetitive 'poor-will' call echoes across desert landscapes, and they're known for calling from the same perches night after night, making them relatively easy to locate for birders.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These grassland raptors undertake one of the longest migrations of any North American bird of prey, traveling over 6,000 miles from their breeding grounds in western North America to wintering areas in Argentina, with some individuals making the journey in just six weeks. They're social migrants who travel in large flocks called 'kettles' that can include thousands of individuals, creating spectacular concentrations at migration bottlenecks like the Isthmus of Panama. These adaptable hunters have learned to follow farm equipment to catch insects stirred up by plowing and harvesting, and they're beneficial to agriculture for consuming vast quantities of grasshoppers, crickets, and other crop pests. They're declining in many areas due to habitat loss and pesticide use, particularly on their wintering grounds where they're vulnerable to agricultural chemicals used on the pampas.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These secretive marsh birds are famous for their spectacular aerial courtship displays where males dive from great heights while their specially modified tail feathers create an eerie winnowing sound that can be heard over half a mile away. They're perfectly adapted for probing in soft mud with flexible bill tips that are packed with nerve endings, allowing them to feel for worms and other invertebrates buried deep in the substrate. These cryptically colored birds are masters of camouflage who freeze motionless when threatened, relying on their streaked plumage to blend perfectly with marsh vegetation, and they often remain hidden until nearly stepped on. They're explosive fliers who burst from cover in a zigzag pattern when flushed, making them challenging targets for hunters and earning them a reputation as one of the most difficult gamebirds to shoot.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These magnificent raptors are the largest hawks in North America and are perfectly adapted to life in open grasslands and prairies, where they hunt primarily for ground squirrels, prairie dogs, and other small mammals. They're ground nesters who build their large stick nests on the ground, on low bushes, or on artificial structures like power poles, and they're known for their impressive nest-building abilities, sometimes creating structures over 3 feet across. These powerful hunters have the largest feet and talons of any North American buteo, allowing them to capture prey as large as jackrabbits and young pronghorn antelope. They're declining across much of their range due to habitat loss and are considered a species of conservation concern, with populations particularly vulnerable to conversion of native grasslands to agriculture.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These powerful falcons are perfectly adapted to hunting in open country, using their incredible speed and agility to chase down ground squirrels, prairie dogs, and birds in spectacular high-speed pursuits across the landscape. They're cliff nesters who prefer to nest on ledges and in cavities on steep rock faces, and they show strong site fidelity, often returning to the same cliff sites for multiple years. These versatile hunters employ multiple hunting strategies including high-speed chases, surprise attacks from low perches, and even hunting on foot when pursuing ground-dwelling prey. They're expanding their range eastward and are increasingly being seen in areas where they were historically absent, possibly taking advantage of habitat changes and the availability of introduced prey species like European Starlings.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These magnificent raptors are among the fastest birds in North America, capable of diving at speeds over 150 mph while hunting, and they're powerful enough to take prey as large as young deer, making them apex predators in many ecosystems. They're incredibly long-lived birds that can survive for over 30 years in the wild, and they often mate for life, with pairs maintaining territories that can span over 60 square miles. These master soaring birds can ride thermals and mountain updrafts for hours without flapping their wings, covering vast distances while scanning for prey with eyesight that's up to eight times sharper than human vision. They're culturally significant birds that have been revered by many Native American tribes and are featured on the coats of arms of numerous countries, symbolizing power, courage, and freedom throughout human history.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These smallest of the thrashers are incredible songsters who can sing continuously for over 22 minutes without taking a break, producing cascades of bubbling notes that echo across the vast sagebrush steppe. They're accomplished mimics who earned the early nickname 'mountain mockingbird' for their ability to imitate other bird species while they sing, weaving borrowed songs into their own complex musical performances. These sagebrush specialists are remarkably adept at finding the best nest sites in seemingly uniform habitat, consistently choosing the densest, tallest shrubs for nesting, with overhead cover that helps protect against aerial predators like Northern Harriers and Loggerhead Shrikes. They're temperature-conscious architects who often orient their nest entrances eastward to capture solar heat during cold desert mornings while providing shade for eggs during the scorching afternoons, demonstrating remarkable adaptation to the extreme daily temperature fluctuations of the high desert.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds

species.description: These spectacular dancing grouse gather at traditional display grounds called leks where males perform mesmerizing courtship displays, bending low with pointed tails skyward while stamping their feet so rapidly they become a blur and inflating purple air sacs to produce quiet cooing sounds. They're culturally significant birds whose spring displays have been incorporated into traditional Native American dances, including the Grouse Dance of the Northern Tutchone people that continues to be practiced in the twenty-first century. These cold-adapted birds grow fleshy projections called pectinae on their toes that act like natural snowshoes, distributing their weight as they walk on unstable surfaces like snowfields, and they sometimes build tunnels through snow for nighttime roosts that provide protection from predators and insulation against extreme cold. They're anatomically named birds placed in genus Tympanuchus, meaning 'drum nape,' referring to their purple air sacs that not only amplify their courtship calls but also serve as displays of overall health and fitness to potential mates.
sources: Cornell Lab of Ornithology All About Birds
